canute.heroSummary: St. Canute IV was king of Denmark from about 1080 until 1086, when rebels killed him, his brother Benedict and seventeen companions in St. Alban's Church in Odense. A forceful ruler and generous supporter of the Church, he was honored as a martyr and canonized in 1101. He is remembered on January 19 and July 10.
canute.searchDescription: St. Canute IV of Denmark, king killed with his brother in an Odense church in 1086 and honored as a martyr. Feast January 19; also remembered July 10.

symbols.meaning: His office as king of Denmark, which he used to support churches and clergy as well as to strengthen royal power.
The weapon of his death; the Catholic Encyclopedia gives the lance as one of his emblems because of how he was killed.
Also recalling his death in St. Alban's Church; accounts of exactly how he was struck differ, so the arrows belong to tradition and art more than to a precise record.

symbols.symbol: Kneeling or slain before an altar
symbols.meaning: Tradition holds that he was killed while praying before the altar; Odense Cathedral notes that a lesion on the skeleton kept there is consistent with that account.

canute.whyWeTurn: People turn to Canute because his story is not simple. He was a strong king who gave generously to the Church, supported its clergy and wanted his kingdom to be Christian, yet his taxes and royal ambitions also stirred anger that ended in revolt. When rebels trapped him in a church at Odense, he prepared for death and died there with his brother. The Church came to honor him as a martyr. Catholics ask his prayers for leaders and anyone who holds authority, that power may serve God and the common good, and for families and nations torn by conflict.

quotes.text: Blessed are they that suffer persecution for justice' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Into thy hands I commend my spirit: thou hast redeemed me, O Lord, the God of truth.

prayer.text: Lord God, you called St. Canute to rule a kingdom and, at the end, to give his life in your house. Through his prayers, guide all who hold authority today, that they may use their power with justice, humility and care for the weak. Heal divisions in families, workplaces and nations, and turn anger into peace. When I am afraid or surrounded by trouble, teach me to come before your altar and place my life in your hands. Make me faithful to you to the end. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: Remember him on January 19, his feast in the older Roman calendar, or on July 10, the anniversary of his death and his date in the Roman Martyrology; he is not on the current General Roman Calendar.
In Denmark, the Catholic calendar of the Diocese of Copenhagen keeps July 10 as his feast in the Danish part of the diocese.
Pray for political leaders and public officials, especially those facing opposition, that they may govern justly and serve the common good.
Pray Psalm 30 (Psalm 31 in other numbering) for someone in danger or distress, recalling the tradition that he died in prayer before the altar.

In Odense, visitors can see the reliquaries traditionally held to contain the remains of Canute and his brother Benedict in the crypt of St. Canute's Cathedral, now a Lutheran (Church of Denmark) cathedral.

places.name: Odense Cathedral (St. Canute's Cathedral)

canute.confirmationNote: Canute may suit a confirmand who expects to lead others, whether in a team, a business or public life, and who wants to think honestly about power. He supported the Church generously, but his reign also shows how authority can provoke resentment and conflict. Choosing his name can be a commitment to use influence for justice, to pray before acting, and to stay faithful to Christ when opposition comes.
reflectionPrompts: Where do I have some authority over others, and do I use it to serve them or mainly to get my own way?
Pray by name for one leader you disagree with this week, and look for one way to lower the temperature of a conflict around you.
Read Psalm 30 and Matthew 5:1–12 in the Douay-Rheims, then read the Catholic Encyclopedia article on St. Canute IV and note how it describes both his reign and his death.

Another king whose faith shaped how he ruled

carlo-acutis.heroSummary: St. Carlo Acutis (1991–2006) was a Milan teenager who went to Mass daily, built websites, and used his computer skills to share the faith, including an exhibition on Eucharistic miracles. He died of leukemia at fifteen, is buried in Assisi, and was canonized by Pope Leo XIV on September 7, 2025. His feast is October 12.
carlo-acutis.searchDescription: St. Carlo Acutis (1991–2006), feast October 12: Milan teenager devoted to the Eucharist who shared the faith online, canonized by Pope Leo XIV in 2025.
carlo-acutis.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Carlo Acutis because his life looks so familiar. He went to school, played soccer and saxophone, filmed his pets, helped classmates with homework, and spent hours at a computer. Yet at the center of his days was the Eucharist: he went to Mass daily and spent time in adoration. He shared his pocket money with poor people in his neighborhood and taught catechism. When leukemia came suddenly, he offered his suffering for the Pope and the Church. Young people, parents, and anyone who works with technology find in him a friend who shows that ordinary life, offered to God, can become holy.

quotes.text: I am the living bread which came down from heaven. If any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever; and the bread that I will give, is my flesh, for the life of the world.
Let no man despise thy youth: but be thou an example of the faithful in word, in conversation, in charity, in faith, in chastity.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, present in the Eucharist, you drew the heart of Saint Carlo to yourself in the ordinary days of school, friendship, and play. Through his prayers, help me to find time for you each day, at Mass when I can and in a quiet word of love when I cannot. Teach me to use my phone, my computer, and every gift I have to bring others closer to you. Give me his kindness toward classmates and his care for the poor, and when suffering comes, let me offer it with trust for your Church. Amen.
prayer.note: Many short sayings are attributed to Carlo; they are not reproduced here because his words are under copyright. The Sanctuary of the Spoliation in Assisi publishes its own prayer.

link.label: Sanctuary of the Spoliation, Assisi (where St. Carlo is buried)

feastCustoms: Keep his feast on October 12, the anniversary of his death; in Assisi the bishop celebrates Mass at the Sanctuary of the Spoliation, and other dioceses and parishes may mark the day as their calendars allow.
Go to Mass on a weekday, or spend some time in Eucharistic adoration, as he did daily.
Explore an exhibition or website on the Church's recognized Eucharistic miracles, the project he researched and designed.
Do one useful thing online for someone else: help a parish with its website, share something true and good, or teach an older relative a digital skill.
Give some of your own money or time to a person in need, as he did with poor people in his Milan neighborhood.

carlo-acutis.confirmationNote: St. Carlo Acutis suits a Confirmation candidate who loves technology, gaming, or creative projects, and who wants faith to fit into an ordinary teenage life. He was confirmed in his Milan parish at twelve and went on to put the Eucharist at the center of his days. Choosing his name can mean committing to regular prayer, kind friendship, and using your skills to share the Gospel.
reflectionPrompts: Where in my ordinary day, at school, at home, or online, could I make a little more room for Jesus?
This week, visit a church for ten minutes of adoration or attend one weekday Mass, and notice how it changes the rest of your day.
Read John 6:22–72 in the Douay-Rheims, then read the life of Carlo in the Holy See's canonization booklet and note how the chapter shaped his devotion.

casimir.heroSummary: St. Casimir is the patron saint of Lithuania and is also honored as a patron of Poland. A son of King Casimir IV, born in Kraków in 1458, he is remembered for prayer, chastity, devotion to Mary and generosity to the poor. He died at twenty-five in 1484, and his feast is March 4.
casimir.searchDescription: St. Casimir (1458–1484), feast March 4: Polish-Lithuanian prince, patron of Lithuania and Poland, remembered for purity, prayer and care for the poor.

symbols.meaning: His purity and his choice to remain unmarried; an old painting in Vilnius, renovated in 1594, already showed him holding a lily.
His royal birth as a son of the king of Poland, and the crowns he might have pursued but did not hold.
His bond with Lithuania, whose grand dukes wore this cap; it marks him as a prince of the Jagiellonian house that ruled both lands.

casimir.whyWeTurn: People turn to Casimir because he lived a quiet holiness in the middle of a royal court. He was a prince with every privilege, yet sources remember him praying at night outside locked church doors, keeping a simple life, caring for the poor and staying chaste when a political marriage was arranged for him. He also governed Poland for a time in his father's absence and was praised for justice. Lithuanians honor him as their principal patron, and young people especially ask his help to stay faithful when status, comfort or pressure from others pull them away from God.

quotes.text: Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God.
Seek ye therefore first the kingdom of God, and his justice, and all these things shall be added unto you.

prayer.text: Lord God, St. Casimir was born to wealth and power, yet he sought your kingdom first. Through his prayers, give me a clean heart and the freedom to say no to what would pull me away from you. Teach me to love the Eucharist and to honor your Mother as he did, and to see the poor as my brothers and sisters. Bless the young people of Lithuania, Poland and every land, and help them stay faithful when the world offers them other crowns. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

link.label: Prayers to St. Casimir from Vilnius Cathedral (in Lithuanian)

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on March 4, his optional memorial in the General Roman Calendar; because the date often falls in Lent, it may be kept as a commemoration that day.

In Vilnius, his feast gave rise to the Kaziukas Fair (Kaziuko mugė), whose traditional sign is the woven Vilnius palm (verba); in the past, processions carried such palms to the cathedral in his honor.
Pray a Marian hymn or the rosary; he loved the long Latin hymn Omni die dic Mariae, though it is older than he is and he did not write it.
Talk with a young person about choosing faith over popularity or status, and pray for young people in Lithuania, whose special patron Pius XII declared him in 1948.
Give alms or fast in his memory, as Lithuanian feast-day customs once did to recall his self-denial and generosity to the poor.

places.name: Vilnius Cathedral Basilica (St. Casimir Chapel)

casimir.confirmationNote: Casimir suits a confirmand who feels pressure to fit in, impress others or chase success. He had wealth, rank and political prospects, yet he gave his first loyalty to God, prayed faithfully, loved Mary and cared for the poor. Pius XII named him a special patron of Lithuanian youth. Choosing his name can be a promise to keep a clean heart and put Christ ahead of status.
reflectionPrompts: What kind of status or approval am I most tempted to chase, and what would it look like to seek God's kingdom first instead?
Set aside one quiet time of prayer before the Blessed Sacrament this week, even briefly, as Casimir sought out churches to pray.
Read Matthew 5:1–12 and 6:19–34 in the Douay-Rheims, then the Catholic Encyclopedia article on St. Casimir, noting what it says about the hymn long attributed to him.

catherine-de-ricci.heroSummary: St. Catherine de' Ricci was a Florentine Dominican nun who led her convent of San Vincenzo in Prato for decades as prioress. She was known for reported weekly ecstasies of Christ's Passion, but also for gentleness with the sick and wise letters to family and friends. She died in 1590 and was canonized in 1746.
catherine-de-ricci.searchDescription: St. Catherine de' Ricci (1522–1590), Dominican feast February 4: the Prato prioress and Passion mystic whose letters offered patient, practical faith.

symbols.meaning: Her life centered on Christ crucified. Her early biographers tell of a crucifix in her cell before which she prayed constantly, and her best-known experiences were weekly ecstasies of the Passion.

Testimony gathered after her death, and her bull of canonization, speak of the marks of the crown of thorns among the signs of the Passion she bore. This belongs to the religious witness about her rather than to independently documented history.
Her biographers describe a ring-shaped mark on her finger, understood as a sign of her mystical espousal to Christ.
Her religious life in the Dominican convent of San Vincenzo at Prato, which she entered as a teenager and served as novice mistress, subprioress and prioress.

catherine-de-ricci.whyWeTurn: People turn to Catherine de' Ricci when suffering feels pointless or family troubles will not go away. She is remembered for extraordinary experiences of Christ's Passion, yet her letters show a sister and daughter worrying about a reckless brother, a sick little half-brother and a father losing his patience. She did not wave their troubles away. She prayed, wrote often and urged patience, trust and peace. As prioress she was known for kindness, especially toward the sick, and Catholic Culture lists her as a patron of sick people. Catholics ask her prayers in illness, in family conflict and whenever they need to unite their own sufferings to Christ's.

quotes.text: May the Divine Majesty grant you patience and give peace to your troubled soul!
quotes.work: Letter to her father, Pierfrancesco de' Ricci, about her brother Ridolfo (1543)
quotes.translation: F. M. Capes, St. Catherine de' Ricci: Her Life, Her Letters, Her Community (1905), public domain

quotes.text: How clearly does not this very trouble prove to you that Jesus loves us and promises us all happiness in order that in the furnace of affliction we may become pure gold!
quotes.work: Letter to her stepmother, Fiammetta da Diacceto, December 30, 1542
quotes.translation: F. M. Capes, St. Catherine de' Ricci: Her Life, Her Letters, Her Community (1905), public domain

quotes.text: With Christ I am nailed to the cross. And I live, now not I; but Christ liveth in me.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, St. Catherine de' Ricci kept your Passion before her eyes and still found room in her heart for her family, her sisters and the sick. Through her prayers, help me to look at your cross when I am suffering and to believe that you are with me there. Give patience and peace to families in conflict, healing and comfort to the sick, and wisdom to all who lead others. Teach me, as she taught her own family, to trust you in every trouble. Amen.

feastCustoms: The Dominican Order celebrates her on February 4; the Roman Martyrology remembers her on February 2, the anniversary of her death. Pray for Dominican nuns and friars on either day.
Spend some time on a Thursday evening or a Friday with the Passion: pray the Stations of the Cross or read one Gospel account of it slowly, as her weekly ecstasies of the Passion recall.
Visit, call or pray for someone who is sick, in honor of her gentleness with the sick as prioress.
Write a letter of encouragement to a family member who is struggling, as she did for her father, stepmother and brothers.
In Prato, where her body rests in the basilica of Santi Vincenzo e Caterina de' Ricci, the local Church keeps her feast with special devotion.
catherine-de-ricci.confirmationNote: Catherine de' Ricci suits a confirmand who is drawn to deep prayer and who wants faith to make a difference at home. She meditated intensely on Christ's suffering, yet she also ran a large community and wrote patient, practical letters to a family full of trouble. Choosing her means asking for a love of the cross that makes us kinder, steadier and more faithful to the people closest to us.
reflectionPrompts: Where in my own family do I most need patience and peace right now?
Write a short note of encouragement this week to a relative who is going through something hard.
Read a few of her letters to her family in F. M. Capes's 1905 St. Catherine de' Ricci: Her Life, Her Letters, Her Community (Internet Archive).

Contemporary in sixteenth-century Italy; tradition says they communicated without ever meeting
Fellow Florentine mystic of the same era, also named in that tradition

Source variance: Catholic Culture gives her canonization as 1747 and her death as 1589 in one place (the review and Catholic Encyclopedia give 1746 and 1590); dominicannuns.org says the Passion ecstasies lasted twenty years and that she was prioress for thirty-six years, while the Catholic Encyclopedia says the weekly ecstasy lasted twelve years. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1908) gives February 13 as her feast, which is the pre-1969 date.

catherine-labour.heroSummary: St. Catherine Labouré was the young Daughter of Charity who, as a novice in Paris in 1830, reported the apparitions of Mary that gave the Church the Miraculous Medal. She then spent more than forty years caring for elderly people at a Paris hospice, almost unknown, and was canonized in 1947.
catherine-labour.searchDescription: St. Catherine Labouré (1806–1876), feast November 28: the Daughter of Charity behind the Miraculous Medal, who served the elderly in hidden faithfulness.

symbols.meaning: The design she reported receiving in 1830: Mary standing on a globe with rays streaming from her hands, framed by the invocation 'O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee.'

symbols.symbol: The letter M with a cross, two hearts and twelve stars
symbols.meaning: The back of the medal: Mary's initial beneath the cross, the Heart of Jesus crowned with thorns and the Heart of Mary pierced by a sword, ringed by twelve stars.

symbols.symbol: Habit of the Daughters of Charity
symbols.meaning: Her vocation in the community founded by Vincent de Paul and Louise de Marillac, which she entered in 1830 and served in until her death.

symbols.symbol: Kneeling beside a chair before Mary
symbols.meaning: Her account of the night of July 18, 1830, when she said she sat at the Virgin's feet in the chapel on the rue du Bac.

catherine-labour.whyWeTurn: People turn to Catherine Labouré when they want Mary's help and when their own life feels small and unseen. The medal linked to her visions spread around the world while she was still alive, yet she kept her role hidden from almost everyone for decades and revealed it only shortly before her death. Meanwhile she cooked, did laundry, kept the door and cared for elderly people at the hospice in Reuilly. Catholics ask her prayers for trust in Mary, for faithfulness in ordinary work, and for anyone who cares for older people. She shows that a great grace and a quiet, humble life can belong together.

quotes.text: And a great sign appeared in heaven: A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars:
Amen I say to you, as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, you gave St. Catherine Labouré a glimpse of your Mother's love and then let her serve you for years in the kitchen, the laundry and the sickrooms of the elderly. Through her prayers, teach me to receive your gifts without seeking attention, and to find you in the small tasks of each day. Bless all who care for the old, the sick and the lonely. And with Catherine I pray: O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee. Amen.
prayer.note: The closing line is the medal's invocation, as quoted by the Central Association of the Miraculous Medal; the Chapel of Our Lady of the Miraculous Medal in Paris renders it 'pray for us who have recourse to you'.

link.label: Novena to Our Lady of the Miraculous Medal (Chapel of Our Lady of the Miraculous Medal, Paris, in French)

feastCustoms: Keep her feast on November 28, the date the Vincentian Family (the Daughters of Charity and the Congregation of the Mission) celebrates her; the Roman Martyrology remembers her on December 31, the day she died.
The day before, November 27, recalls the 1830 apparition of the medal and is kept in some places as Our Lady of the Miraculous Medal; it makes a natural two-day observance.
Wear a Miraculous Medal, or give one to someone who is struggling, and pray its short invocation during the day.
Visit or call an older relative or neighbor, or volunteer at a care home, in honor of her decades with the elderly at Reuilly.
Do one hidden job well without telling anyone, as she did for most of her life.

catherine-labour.confirmationNote: Catherine Labouré suits a confirmand who loves Mary and who suspects that holiness is mostly quiet. She received a gift that touched millions, then spent her life doing ordinary work for elderly people without seeking credit. Choosing her means asking for a deep trust in Mary, a humble heart, and the patience to serve faithfully when no one is watching.
reflectionPrompts: Is there something good God has done in my life that I want people to notice, and can I let it be enough that he knows?
Spend an hour this week with an older person, listening more than talking.

catherine-of-alexandria.heroSummary: St. Catherine of Alexandria is a traditional patron of lawyers, philosophers and students. Her legend tells of a learned young Christian who out-argued an emperor's scholars and broke a spiked wheel. Her feast left the General Roman Calendar in 1969 and returned in 2002 as an optional memorial on November 25.
catherine-of-alexandria.searchDescription: St. Catherine of Alexandria, November 25: the legendary scholar-martyr of the wheel, patron of lawyers and students, restored to the calendar in 2002.

symbols.meaning: Her legend says she was sentenced to die on a wheel set with blades, which shattered when she touched it. It became her best-known emblem, and wheelwrights and mechanics took her as patron because of it.
The legend ends with her beheading after the wheel failed; the sword marks her death as a martyr.
Her learning. In the story she defended the faith so well that the philosophers sent to refute her were converted, which is why scholars, preachers and students invoke her.
Often placed at her feet or on her head. It signals both the noble rank her legend gives her and the martyr's crown of victory.
A later legend of her 'mystical marriage' to Christ, a way of picturing her life as wholly given to him. This detail is tradition, not history.

catherine-of-alexandria.whyWeTurn: People turn to Catherine of Alexandria when they have to think hard, speak clearly or defend what they believe. Almost nothing about her life can be confirmed, and the Church says so honestly: her story reached the West mainly through medieval legend. Yet tradition holds her up as a young woman whose faith and intelligence worked together, and for centuries philosophers, theologians and preachers asked her prayers before they studied, wrote or preached. Students facing exams, lawyers preparing a case and anyone asked to explain their faith can still borrow that prayer: for a clear mind, honest words and the courage not to back down.

quotes.text: For I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to resist and gainsay.
But sanctify the Lord Christ in your hearts, being ready always to satisfy every one that asketh you a reason of that hope which is in you.

prayer.text: Lord God, the Church has long honored St. Catherine of Alexandria as a young woman who loved truth and would not deny you. Through her prayers, give students, teachers, lawyers and all who study a clear mind and an honest heart. When I am asked about my faith, give me words that are true, gentle and unafraid. Keep me from pride in what I know, and let all my learning lead me closer to your Son, the Word made flesh, who lives and reigns with you for ever and ever. Amen.
prayer.note: The Roman Missal has a proper collect for her optional memorial, but its current English text is copyrighted, so an original prayer is given here.

feastCustoms: Since 2002 the Roman Missal again has an optional memorial for her on November 25; check whether your parish is celebrating it, or pray the day's Mass readings at home.
Before an exam, a presentation or a hard conversation about faith, ask her prayers for a clear mind and the right words.
Read 1 Peter 3:15 and practice explaining one thing you believe, simply and kindly, to a friend.
Bake St. Catherine's wigs or another traditional St. Catherine treat; Catholic Culture's November 25 page links recipes.
Among Dominicans she is honored as a special patroness of the Order, especially of those studying philosophy; pray for students and teachers in Catholic schools and universities.
catherine-of-alexandria.confirmationNote: Catherine of Alexandria suits a confirmand who loves to learn, argue and ask big questions. Her story is legend, and the Church admits that openly, but Christians have long seen in her a faith that thinks. Choosing her means asking the Holy Spirit for wisdom and courage: to study the faith seriously, and to explain it with honesty and respect when others push back.
reflectionPrompts: Which question about my faith do I avoid because I am afraid I cannot answer it?
Choose one question a friend might ask about the Catholic faith and write a short, honest answer to it this week.
Read the 1907 Catholic Encyclopedia article on St. Catherine of Alexandria and note what it treats as certain and what it calls later embellishment.

catherine-of-genoa.heroSummary: St. Catherine of Genoa is honored in Catholic patronage lists as a patron of hospitals, fitting for a laywoman who spent years caring for the sick at Genoa's Pammatone Hospital and helping to run it. Unhappily married at sixteen, she was converted in 1473 and became a mystic of God's purifying love. Her feast is September 15.
catherine-of-genoa.searchDescription: St. Catherine of Genoa, feast September 15: a married laywoman and mystic who served the sick at Genoa's hospital and taught that purgatory is purifying love.
catherine-of-genoa.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Catherine of Genoa when prayer and practical service seem to pull in opposite directions. Benedict XVI pointed out that her intense life of prayer never pulled her away from the sick she served in Genoa's great hospital, where she kept the accounts as carefully as she tended patients. She also knew years of loneliness in a difficult marriage, and her husband's eventual change of heart shows that such stories need not end in despair. Many Catholics also remember her when they pray for the dead, because her teaching presents purgatory as the fire of God's love cleansing a soul for joy, not as a place of cruelty.

quotes.text: There is no peace to be compared with that of the souls in purgatory, save that of the saints in paradise, and this peace is ever augmented by the inflowing of God into these souls.
quotes.work: Treatise on Purgatory, chapter 2 (as compiled by her circle after her death)
quotes.translation: Life and Doctrine of Saint Catherine of Genoa, translated from the Italian (New York: Christian Press Association, 1907; public domain)

quotes.text: As a covered surface can never reflect the sun, not through any defect in that orb, but simply from the resistance offered by the covering, so, if the covering be gradually removed, the surface will by little and little be opened to the sun and will more and more reflect his light.
quotes.work: Treatise on Purgatory, chapter 2 (as compiled by her circle after her death)
quotes.translation: Life and Doctrine of Saint Catherine of Genoa, translated from the Italian (New York: Christian Press Association, 1907; public domain)

quotes.text: O Lord! no more world, no more sin.
quotes.work: Life of St. Catherine of Genoa, account of her conversion (words her biographers attribute to her)
quotes.translation: Life and Doctrine of Saint Catherine of Genoa, translated from the Italian (New York: Christian Press Association, 1907; public domain)

prayer.text: Loving God, you set the heart of St. Catherine of Genoa on fire with your love and sent her to serve the sick with patient, practical care. Through her prayers, help me to love you in quiet prayer and to find you again in the people who need me. Strengthen all who work in hospitals and all who wait in sickness. Comfort those whose marriages are lonely or wounded, and do not let them lose hope. Have mercy on the faithful departed; purify them by your love and bring them into the light of your presence. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: Remember her on September 15, the date of her death in 1510 and of her listing in Catholic calendars. In the General Roman Calendar that day belongs to Our Lady of Sorrows, so her day is usually kept in personal or family prayer.
Read the first two chapters of her Treatise on Purgatory and pray for the dead, especially those who have no one to pray for them.
Visit someone who is sick, or give some time or support to a local hospital, hospice or nursing home, as she served the sick in Genoa.
Read Benedict XVI's general audience on St. Catherine of Genoa (January 12, 2011), which links her mystical teaching with her daily work for the sick.

In Genoa, pilgrims visit her incorrupt body in the upper chapel of the church of the Santissima Annunziata di Portoria, popularly called the church of Santa Caterina, which stands beside the site of the old Pammatone Hospital.

places.name: Church of Santissima Annunziata di Portoria (Santa Caterina da Genova) and Capuchin Museum

catherine-of-genoa.confirmationNote: Catherine suits a confirmand who wants a faith that is both prayerful and hands-on, especially someone drawn to nursing, medicine or care for others. She came to a living faith after years of unhappiness, then spent herself serving the sick without letting go of prayer. Confirmation gives the Holy Spirit's gifts for that kind of life, and her example shows that loving God and caring for people belong together.
reflectionPrompts: Is there a part of my life where I keep prayer and service in separate boxes, and how might they belong together?

catherine-of-siena.heroSummary: St. Catherine of Siena is a co-patron of Europe and a patron of Italy and of nurses. A fourteenth-century Dominican laywoman, she cared for the sick, urged Pope Gregory XI to return from Avignon to Rome, and dictated the Dialogue. Paul VI declared her a Doctor of the Church in 1970, and her feast is April 29.
catherine-of-siena.searchDescription: St. Catherine of Siena (1347–1380), feast April 29: Dominican laywoman, Doctor of the Church, and co-patron of Europe and patron of Italy.

symbols.meaning: Her consecration of her life to God as a virgin.

symbols.symbol: Dominican habit, white tunic and black mantle
symbols.meaning: She belonged to the Mantellate, Dominican laywomen who lived at home while following the Order's spirituality.
Her concentration on Christ crucified, whom she urged her correspondents again and again to remember.
Raymond of Capua's account of her mystical espousal, in which Christ gave her a ring that only she could see, a sign of faithful union with him.
Her followers' testimony that she shared in Christ's wounds; this belongs to the religious witness about her rather than to independently documented history.

catherine-of-siena.whyWeTurn: People turn to Catherine when the Church or the world feels divided and they want to help heal it. She was a young laywoman, yet she wrote to popes, rulers, and ordinary friends, urging repentance, peace, and courage, and she called the pope the "sweet Christ on earth" while still challenging him to act. She cared for sick people with her own hands, one reason nurses look to her. Her love for the Church was fierce enough to criticize its leaders and loyal enough never to leave it. Catholics ask her prayers for Church unity, for Europe and Italy, and for anyone called to speak hard truths with charity.

quotes.text: Wherefore I have told thee that I have made a Bridge of My Word, of My only-begotten Son, and this is the truth.
quotes.work: The Dialogue, A Treatise of Discretion (God the Father speaking to Catherine)

quotes.text: Thou, oh eternal Trinity, art a deep Sea, into which the deeper I enter the more I find, and the more I find the more I seek; the soul cannot be satiated in Thy abyss, for she continually hungers after Thee
quotes.work: The Dialogue, A Treatise of Obedience, closing prayer

quotes.text: If you are what you ought to be, you will set fire to all Italy, and not only yonder.
quotes.translation: Vida D. Scudder, Saint Catherine of Siena as Seen in Her Letters (1905), public domain

prayer.text: Oh! Abyss, oh! Eternal Godhead, oh! Sea Profound! what more couldst Thou give me than Thyself, Thou art the fire which ever burns without being consumed; Thou consumest in Thy heat all the soul's self-love; Thou art the fire which takes away all cold; with Thy light Thou dost illuminate me so that I may know all Thy truth.
prayer.source: St. Catherine of Siena, The Dialogue, closing prayer of A Treatise of Obedience, translated by Algar Thorold (1907)
prayer.note: An excerpt from the thanksgiving prayer with which the Dialogue ends, in Thorold's 1907 wording exactly. Some online editions modernize "Thou" to "You."

Visit or help someone who is sick, or thank a nurse, in honor of her care for the sick.
Read the Dialogue's image of Christ the Bridge and pray over one step of it.
Write a letter of honest encouragement to someone, as she did in hundreds of letters to friends, rulers, and popes.

catherine-of-siena.confirmationNote: Catherine suits a Confirmation candidate who cares about justice, peace, and the health of the Church, and who is not afraid to speak up. She was young, a layperson, and deeply prayerful, and her courage came from time spent with Christ. Choosing her means committing to prayer, to serving the sick and needy, and to speaking honestly but charitably, even to people in authority.

cecilia.heroSummary: St. Cecilia is the patron of church music and of musicians. She was an early Roman virgin martyr buried in the Catacomb of Callistus beside the crypt of the popes, and her church in Trastevere dates to the fourth century. Her name is in the Roman Canon, and her memorial is November 22.
cecilia.searchDescription: St. Cecilia, feast November 22: Roman virgin martyr and patron of church music, buried beside the popes in the Callistus catacomb and named in the Roman Canon.

symbols.meaning: Her ordinary attribute since the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. It comes from the line in her Acts that while instruments played at her wedding she sang to God alone in her heart; later readers seem to have taken her for the organist herself.
Like the organ, a sign of her patronage of music, which spread after she was named patroness of the music academy founded in Rome in 1584.

From the fifth-century Acts, which say an angel crowned Cecilia and her husband Valerian with roses and lilies after his baptism. This is legend; the lilies speak of purity and the roses of martyrdom.
The oldest images of her, such as the sixth-century mosaic at Sant'Apollinare Nuovo in Ravenna, show her holding the crown given to martyrs.

symbols.symbol: Lying on her side with a wounded neck
symbols.meaning: Stefano Maderno's 1599 marble statue under the high altar of her church in Trastevere shows her as she fell under the executioner's blows. The Acts say the sword struck three times and she lived three days; this detail is tradition.

cecilia.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Cecilia whenever music is offered to God: choir members, organists, cantors, music teachers and anyone who sings at Mass. Tradition holds that while instruments played at her wedding feast, she sang in her heart to the Lord alone, and from that image the Church came to see her as the patron of sacred music. History tells us less than the legend, but it is clear that Rome honored her very early, buried her beside the popes and built a church in her name. She reminds us that what matters is the song of the heart. Many also ask her prayers for courage and purity.

quotes.text: Let my heart be undefiled in thy justifications, that I may not be confounded.
quotes.work: Psalm 118:80 (the verse her traditional antiphon has her singing in her heart)

quotes.text: Speaking to yourselves in psalms, and hymns, and spiritual canticles, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord.

prayer.text: Lord God, St. Cecilia sang to you in her heart and gave you her whole life, even unto death. Through her prayers, bless all who lead your people in song: organists, cantors, choirs, composers and music teachers. Let our music at Mass be humble, beautiful and true, sung to you and not for our own praise. Keep my heart undefiled and unafraid, so that in good times and hard times I may still praise you. Bring us at last to sing with her and all the saints in your kingdom. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on November 22, the memorial of St. Cecilia, Virgin and Martyr, in the General Roman Calendar; in years when it falls on a Sunday, the Sunday celebration takes its place. Listen for her name if the priest uses Eucharistic Prayer I.
Hold a family evening of singing or playing instruments, or listen together to Gregorian chant and sacred polyphony, as Catholic Culture suggests.
Thank and pray for your parish organist, cantors and choir, or join the choir yourself.
In Rome, her feast is kept at the Basilica of Santa Cecilia in Trastevere, where her relics lie under the high altar, and at her original crypt in the Catacomb of St. Callistus on the Via Appia.

Read a Church document on sacred music, such as St. John Paul II's chirograph for the centenary of Tra le sollecitudini, which he signed on her memorial in 2003, and reflect on what music at Mass is for.

cecilia.confirmationNote: Cecilia suits a confirmand who sings, plays an instrument or simply loves music, and who wants a patron for using that gift in praise of God. Tradition remembers her singing to the Lord in her heart while the world celebrated around her, and Rome honored her as a martyr from very early times. Confirmation strengthens Christians to bear witness, and her example shows that a gift offered to God can become a witness in itself.

cesario.heroSummary: St. Caesarius of Nazianzus was the younger brother of St. Gregory of Nazianzus, a physician trained at Alexandria who served at the imperial court and refused Julian the Apostate's pressure to give up his faith. Spared in the Nicaea earthquake of 368, he was baptized, then died soon after of illness, leaving his goods to the poor.
cesario.searchDescription: St. Caesarius of Nazianzus, feast February 25: physician brother of St. Gregory who stood firm before Julian the Apostate and left his goods to the poor.
cesario.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Caesarius when their work puts them close to power and their faith is quietly tested. His brother Gregory tells us that he treated the authorities without charge, that he cared more about being known as a Christian than about any honor, and that when Julian the Apostate tried to argue him out of his faith, he answered that he was and remained a Christian. Doctors, nurses and public servants find in him a colleague. So do people who have put off a full commitment to God: shaken by surviving an earthquake, Caesarius was baptized and gave his heart to God before his early death.

quotes.text: He himself cared most for being, and being known to be, a Christian, and, compared with this, all other things were to him but trifling toys.
quotes.work: St. Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 7 (Panegyric on His Brother St. Caesarius), section 10
quotes.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 7 (1894; public domain)

quotes.text: Cæsarius in a loud clear voice declared that he was and remained a Christian.
quotes.work: St. Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 7, section 13 (on his debate with Julian the Apostate)
quotes.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 7 (1894; public domain)

quotes.text: While the only real and securely abiding good thing is godliness.
quotes.work: St. Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 7, section 10
quotes.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 7 (1894; public domain)

prayer.text: Lord God, you gave St. Caesarius skill in healing and the courage to say, before an emperor, that he was and remained a Christian. Through his prayers, bless all who care for the sick, and all whose work brings them close to wealth and power. Keep us from valuing honors more than you. Wake us, as you woke him, from putting off our full surrender to you, and teach us to share what we have with the poor. Console families who mourn a brother or sister, and bring us all at last to the life that does not end. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: Remember him on February 25, his commemoration in Western calendars (the Greek churches keep March 9). He is not on the General Roman Calendar, so this is a day for personal or family prayer.
Read St. Gregory of Nazianzus's funeral oration for him (Oration 7), especially sections 10 to 15, freely available online in the 1894 translation.
Pray for physicians, nurses and others in healthcare, especially those who face pressure at work to set aside their conscience.
Give something to the poor in his memory, since he asked that his goods be distributed to them.
Pray for anyone you know who has been putting off baptism, confession or a return to the faith.
cesario.confirmationNote: Caesarius suits a confirmand who loves science or medicine, or who expects a demanding career among powerful people. His brother says he excelled in his studies and his profession, yet cared most about being known as a Christian, and he told an emperor so to his face. Confirmation strengthens Christians to bear witness wherever they work, and his example shows that talent and faith can serve the same Lord.
reflectionPrompts: What honor, job or approval am I most tempted to value more than being known as a Christian?
This week, thank a doctor, nurse or caregiver who has helped you, and pray for them by name.
Read St. Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 7, sections 10–15, and St. Basil's Letter 26 to Caesarius after the earthquake, and compare how the two friends saw his escape.

chaeremon.heroSummary: St. Chaeremon was an elderly bishop of Nilopolis in Egypt during the persecution of Decius, about 250. His fellow bishop Dionysius of Alexandria wrote that he fled with his wife into the Arabian mountains and never returned, and that searchers found neither them nor their bodies. The Church remembers him on December 22.
chaeremon.searchDescription: St. Chaeremon of Nilopolis, December 22: an aged Egyptian bishop who fled the Decian persecution with his wife and vanished in the Arabian mountains.
chaeremon.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Chaeremon when someone they love has disappeared, or when they have been forced to leave home with no idea how the story will end. Dionysius of Alexandria tells us only that this old bishop fled with his wife, that they never came back, and that the community searched for them without success. There are no heroic last words, only absence and grief, and the Church still counts him among the martyrs. Refugees, families of the missing, elderly people who must start over, and Christians who live under persecution today can find in him a companion who knows uncertainty from the inside.

quotes.text: Chæremon, who was very old, was bishop of the city called Nilus. He fled with his wife to the Arabian mountain and did not return. And though the brethren searched diligently they could not find either them or their bodies.
quotes.work: Dionysius of Alexandria, letter to Fabius of Antioch, in Eusebius, Church History VI.42.3
quotes.translation: Arthur Cushman McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 1 (1890; public domain)

quotes.text: Why need I speak of the multitude that wandered in the deserts and mountains, and perished by hunger, and thirst, and cold, and sickness, and robbers, and wild beasts? Those of them who survived are witnesses of their election and victory.
quotes.work: Dionysius of Alexandria, in Eusebius, Church History VI.42.2
quotes.translation: Arthur Cushman McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 1 (1890; public domain)

prayer.text: Lord God, St. Chaeremon and his wife fled from persecution and were never seen again, yet you knew where they were and received them. Through his prayers, comfort all families who are searching for someone they love, and all who have had to flee their homes because of violence or their faith. Give courage to elderly people whose lives are turned upside down. Help us to welcome refugees with mercy, and to remember persecuted Christians in our prayers. When we cannot see how a story ends, teach us to trust it to you. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: Remember him on December 22, his commemoration in the Roman Martyrology. He is not on the General Roman Calendar, so this is a day for personal or family prayer in the last days of Advent.
Read Eusebius, Church History VI.41–42, where Dionysius of Alexandria describes the Decian persecution in Egypt, including Chaeremon's flight.
Pray for refugees and displaced people, and support a parish or Catholic agency that helps them.
Pray for families of missing persons and for people who have disappeared in war or persecution.
Pray for Christians who are persecuted for their faith today, and learn about one place where that is happening.
chaeremon.confirmationNote: Chaeremon suits a confirmand who has known loss, displacement or an unanswered question, or who feels drawn to help refugees and persecuted Christians. His story offers no dramatic ending, only a faithful old man who left everything rather than deny Christ. Confirmation strengthens Christians to bear witness in every circumstance, and his example shows that faithfulness counts even when no one sees how the story ends.
reflectionPrompts: Where in my life do I have to trust God without knowing how things will turn out?
This week, pray for refugees by name or by country, and find one practical way to support people who have had to flee their homes.
Read Eusebius, Church History VI.41–42, and note how Dionysius distinguishes what he saw, what he heard and what remained unknown.

symbols.meaning: His profession in the Lebanese Maronite Order, which he entered in 1851 and served as monk, priest, and finally hermit.
The way he is usually shown, commonly understood as a sign of his recollection and hidden life of prayer.
The aged hermit of his final decades, living in solitude at the Hermitage of Sts. Peter and Paul above the monastery until his death at about seventy.

charbel-makhlouf.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Charbel because he shows that a hidden life can carry great weight. He was a mountain villager who became a monk, served for years in an ordinary community, and then asked to live alone in prayer, work, and penance. He died almost unknown on Christmas Eve 1898. Since then, many people have reported healings and answered prayers at his tomb, and Christians, Muslims, Druze, and others come to Annaya to pray. Pope Leo XIV, the first pope to pray there, said that Charbel teaches prayer, silence, humility, and freedom from wealth to a noisy world. Anyone longing for quiet and for God can find in him a patient friend.

quotes.text: Come to me, all you that labour, and are burdened, and I will refresh you.
Be still and see that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, and I will be exalted in the earth.

prayer.text: Lord God, you drew Saint Charbel away from noise and into the silence where he could listen to you. Through his prayers, quiet my restless heart and teach me to give you time each day, even when I feel I have none. Help me to work honestly, to live simply, and to love the Eucharist as he did. Bring healing to the sick, peace to Lebanon and the whole Middle East, and friendship among people of different faiths. Like him, may I seek to please you rather than to be noticed. Amen.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on July 24, his optional memorial; Catholic Culture notes that it was added to the calendar of the United States in 2004.
Set aside a stretch of real silence for prayer, away from your phone and other noise, in the spirit of his hermit life.
Pray for peace in Lebanon and the Middle East, the intention Pope Leo XIV entrusted to St. Charbel at his tomb in December 2025.
Learn about the Maronite Church, an Eastern Catholic Church with its own liturgy, or visit a Maronite parish if there is one near you.
At Annaya, pilgrims gather on the 22nd of each month to pray at the monastery and tomb, a custom described by CNEWA.
charbel-makhlouf.confirmationNote: St. Charbel can suit a Confirmation candidate who feels drawn to prayer and quiet, or who has Lebanese or Maronite roots. He chose a hidden, disciplined life, yet his witness now reaches people of many faiths. Taking his name can mean committing to make room for silence with God, to work faithfully without seeking attention, and to pray for peace in a divided world.
reflectionPrompts: Where in my day is there real silence, and what would it take to give a few minutes of it to God?
This week, take ten minutes of quiet prayer each day with your phone in another room, and notice what changes.
Read Matthew 11:25–30 in the Douay-Rheims, then read Vatican News's account of Pope Leo XIV's prayer at St. Charbel's tomb (December 2025) and note the four lessons he drew from the saint.

charles-borromeo.heroSummary: St. Charles Borromeo (1538–1584) was a cardinal and archbishop of Milan who helped bring the Council of Trent to its close and then put its reforms into practice. He founded seminaries, visited his parishes, and cared for the sick during the plague of 1576–77. His memorial is November 4.
charles-borromeo.searchDescription: St. Charles Borromeo (1538–1584), archbishop of Milan who carried out the Council of Trent's reforms and served the sick in the plague. Feast: November 4.

symbols.meaning: The penitential processions of the 1576 plague, when he walked barefoot with a rope around his neck to atone for his people's sins and plead for mercy.
His role as archbishop leading those same plague processions, and his personal care for the sick and dying.
His appointment as cardinal as a young man by his uncle, Pope Pius IV, and his service in Rome during the last phase of the Council of Trent.

symbols.symbol: The word Humilitas under a crown
symbols.meaning: Humility, the motto of his family and of his episcopate, a reminder that rank was to be put at the service of others.

charles-borromeo.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Charles Borromeo because he took a powerful position and used it to serve. Born into wealth and made a cardinal while still young, he could have lived comfortably. Instead he chose the priesthood, moved to Milan to live among his people, and spent himself on reform: training priests, teaching children the faith, and visiting his parishes again and again. When famine and plague struck, he stayed, gave away his goods, and cared for the sick himself. He survived an attempt on his life and died worn out at forty-six. Bishops, priests, seminarians, catechists, and anyone charged with renewing a tired community find in him a model of steady, practical holiness.

quotes.text: Then said I, Behold I come. In the head of the book it is written of me that I should do thy will: O my God, I have desired it, and thy law in the midst of my heart.
I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd giveth his life for his sheep.
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking care of it, not by constraint, but willingly, according to God: not for filthy lucre's sake, but voluntarily.

prayer.text: Lord God, you gave Saint Charles Borromeo a heart for the renewal of your Church and the courage to stay with his people in time of plague. Through his prayers, renew your Church in our day. Give our bishops and priests his humility and zeal, strengthen seminarians and all who teach the faith, and help me to use whatever gifts and resources I have in the service of others. When I am tempted to put comfort first, remind me that every good work begins with prayer. Amen.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on November 4, his memorial in the General Roman Calendar; in Milan Cathedral, where his body rests, the day is kept as a solemnity.
Pray for your bishop and parish priests, and for vocations to the priesthood, as Catholic Culture suggests for his feast.
Teach someone a piece of the faith or give a good Catholic book, remembering his work for the catechism and for teaching children.
Learn about the Council of Trent and how its decisions reached ordinary parishes.
Some families serve Milanese dishes such as risotto alla milanese or panettone; Catholic Culture also notes that St. John Paul II, baptized Karol, kept this day as his name day.

places.name: Milan Cathedral (Duomo di Milano), Scurolo di San Carlo, the crypt chapel holding his body

charles-borromeo.confirmationNote: St. Charles Borromeo can suit a Confirmation candidate who likes to organize, lead, or fix what is broken, or who is drawn to teaching the faith. He had every advantage of wealth and rank, yet he chose humility and spent himself on renewing the Church and caring for the sick. Taking his name can mean committing to serve your parish with real work, not just good intentions.
reflectionPrompts: What advantages or gifts have I been given, and am I using them for myself or for others?
Offer an hour this month to a parish need, such as helping with religious education, visiting someone sick, or supporting a parish project.
Read John 10:1–18 in the Douay-Rheims, then the 1908 Catholic Encyclopedia article on St. Charles Borromeo, and note how he tried to act as a good shepherd in Milan.

charles-lwanga.heroSummary: St. Charles Lwanga led and protected the young Christian pages at the court of King Mwanga II of Buganda. Baptized in 1885, he encouraged them under persecution and was burned to death at Namugongo on June 3, 1886. He and his twenty-one companions, canonized in 1964, are honored together on June 3.
charles-lwanga.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Charles Lwanga because he stood between vulnerable young people and the power that threatened them. As head of the royal pages, he taught them the faith, kept them steady, and baptized catechumens when death was close. The persecution involved both hostility to Christianity and the king's sexual coercion of the pages, and together they refused to surrender their faith or their dignity. He was about twenty-five when he died. Young people under pressure, those who guard and mentor them, survivors of abuse, and Christians facing hostility find in him a friend who was brave on behalf of others, not only for himself.

quotes.text: But you shall receive the power of the Holy Ghost coming upon you, and you shall be witnesses unto me in Jerusalem, and in all Judea, and Samaria, and even to the uttermost part of the earth.
And fear ye not them that kill the body, and are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him that can destroy both soul and body in hell.
Who then shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation? or distress? or famine? or nakedness? or danger? or persecution? or the sword?

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, Saint Charles Lwanga cared for the young people entrusted to him and would not let fear take you from them. Through his prayers and those of his companions, protect children and young people from every kind of abuse and exploitation, and give courage to those who stand up for them. Strengthen Christians who suffer for their faith, and draw Catholics and Anglicans closer together, as the martyrs of Uganda were united in their death. Make me a faithful witness at home, at school, and at work. Amen.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on June 3, the memorial of Sts. Charles Lwanga and Companions in the General Roman Calendar.
Join in spirit with the great pilgrimage to the Basilica of the Uganda Martyrs at Namugongo, where very large crowds gather each June 3, many having walked for days or come from other countries.
Pray for children and young people who are pressured, exploited, or abused, and for the adults who protect them.
Pray for Christian unity, remembering the Anglican martyrs of the same persecution, whom Pope Francis honored as part of an 'ecumenism of blood.'
Learn about the Church in Uganda and in Africa today, or support a mission or youth group there.

places.name: Uganda Martyrs Catholic Shrine, Namugongo (its altar stands on the site of his martyrdom)

charles-lwanga.confirmationNote: St. Charles Lwanga can suit a Confirmation candidate who looks out for younger people, who is a leader among friends, or who has African roots. He used his position to teach, encourage, and shield others, and he refused to give up either his faith or his dignity. Taking his name can mean committing to protect people more vulnerable than you and to stay faithful under pressure.
reflectionPrompts: Who looks up to me, and how am I helping them stay faithful and safe?
This week, do one concrete thing to encourage or stand up for someone younger or more vulnerable than you.
Read Acts 1:1–11 in the Douay-Rheims, then Pope Francis's homily at the Namugongo shrine (28 November 2015) on vatican.va, and note what he says it means to honor the martyrs today.

charles-of-mount-argus.heroSummary: St. Charles of Mount Argus was a Dutch Passionist priest, born Johannes Andreas Houben, who spent most of his ministry at Mount Argus in Dublin. His English was never good enough for formal preaching, so he served through confession, counsel and blessing the sick, and crowds sought him out. Benedict XVI canonized him in 2007; his feast is January 5.
charles-of-mount-argus.searchDescription: St. Charles of Mount Argus, a Dutch Passionist in Dublin, heard confessions and blessed the sick for decades. Canonized in 2007; feast January 5.
charles-of-mount-argus.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Charles when they are sick or carrying a heavy sorrow. He never mastered English well enough to preach, yet people came to him in great numbers, because he listened, heard confessions and blessed them with obvious compassion. Benedict XVI said he saw the face of the crucified Christ in the sick and suffering. Reports of healings followed him, but his deeper gift was a faith that suffering joined to Christ's Passion is never wasted. He is a reminder that a limitation, even in something as basic as language, need not limit what God can do through us. Many still bring their intentions to his tomb in Dublin.

quotes.text: But he was wounded for our iniquities, he was bruised for our sins: the chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his bruises we are healed.

Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith shall save the sick man: and the Lord shall raise him up.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus Christ, St. Charles of Mount Argus saw your face in the sick and found his strength in your Passion. Through his prayers, look with mercy on all who are ill in body, mind or spirit, especially those I name before you now. Give them healing according to your will, and the peace of knowing that you suffer with them. Make me patient with my own weakness and gentle with the weakness of others. Like Charles, may I serve wherever I am sent, even when I feel unequal to the task, and trust you to do what I cannot. Amen.

feastCustoms: Remember him on January 5, his memorial in the Passionist calendar; at Mount Argus in Dublin the feast is marked with Mass and blessings with his relic.
If you are in Dublin, pray at his tomb inside the Mount Argus church, where his remains were moved in 1949.
Pray by name for someone who is sick, and if you can, visit them or help them ask a priest for the Anointing of the Sick.
Make a good confession; hearing confessions and giving counsel were at the center of his ministry.
Spend a few minutes before a crucifix meditating on Christ's Passion, the devotion at the heart of Passionist life.

places.name: Mount Argus Church, Passionist parish and site of his tomb

charles-of-mount-argus.confirmationNote: Charles suits a confirmand who feels unsure of their gifts, or who is drawn to care for the sick. He was a foreigner who never mastered the language of the people he served, yet God worked powerfully through his compassion, prayer and patience. Choosing him means trusting that the Holy Spirit works through faithfulness more than talent, and committing to bring Christ's comfort to people who suffer.
reflectionPrompts: What limitation in myself do I assume keeps God from using me?
This week, visit, call or write to someone who is sick, and promise to pray for them by name.
Read Isaias (Isaiah) 53 in the Douay-Rheims alongside Benedict XVI's canonization homily of June 3, 2007, and note how each links suffering and healing.

christopher.heroSummary: St. Christopher is a patron of motorists and travelers, honored by the Church as an early Christian martyr. Almost nothing is documented about his life; the famous story of a giant carrying the Christ Child across a river is a legend built on his name, which means "Christ-bearer." His traditional Western date is July 25.
christopher.searchDescription: St. Christopher, patron of motorists and travelers, is an early martyr remembered July 25. Learn what is history and what is legend in his story.

symbols.meaning: His name means "Christ-bearer." The legend says he carried a child across a river who grew as heavy as the world and revealed himself as Christ; the image is legend, not documented history.
The dangerous water where, tradition holds, he carried travelers across as his service to Christ; it stands for the hazards of every journey.
The staff he leaned on in the crossing, which in the legend later sprouts like a tree as a sign; Catholic Culture lists tree and branch among his attributes.
The legend makes him a giant who set out to serve the strongest master he could find; his size shows great strength turned into humble service.
A puzzling Eastern image; Vatican News notes theories about its origin and favors a Christian reading rather than a pagan one. It is iconographic tradition, not a claim about his appearance.

christopher.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Christopher before a journey. Tradition holds that he carried travelers across a dangerous river, and that one small passenger grew as heavy as the whole world because he was Christ. Whether or not it happened that way, the story says something true: anyone who serves others along the road is carrying Christ. The Church still lists Christopher among the martyrs, and Catholics ask his prayers for safe travel, for drivers and transport workers, and for anyone facing a crossing whose far shore they cannot yet see. A St. Christopher medal in the car is a reminder to pray and to drive with care, not a lucky charm.

quotes.text: Bear ye one another's burdens; and so you shall fulfill the law of Christ.
Come to me, all you that labour, and are burdened, and I will refresh you.
For my yoke is sweet and my burden light.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus Christ, St. Christopher's name means one who carries you. Through his prayers, protect all who travel today: drivers and passengers, pilots and sailors, and everyone who works on our roads. Keep us alert, patient and courteous, and turn our hearts from haste and anger. When the way ahead is dark or the current runs strong, give us strength to keep going and faith that you are with us. Help us carry you to every person we meet along the way, and bring us safely home, and at last to our home with you. Amen.

feastCustoms: Remember him on July 25, his traditional Western date. Since the 1969 calendar reform his commemoration belongs only to local calendars, so most parishes celebrate St. James the Apostle at Mass that day.
Bring your car to a blessing of vehicles; some parishes, especially those named for him, offer one on or near July 25.
Before a trip, pray together for everyone in the car and for others on the road; the Book of Blessings includes a blessing of travelers.
Carry or give a St. Christopher medal as a reminder to pray and drive with care, not as a good-luck charm.
With children, tell the river story as a legend and talk about how helping others can be a way of carrying Christ.
christopher.confirmationNote: Christopher suits a confirmand who is strong, practical and drawn to helping others, or who spends much of life on the road. Choosing him means choosing a martyr whose life is mostly hidden and whose best-known story is legend. That need not be an obstacle: his name, Christ-bearer, describes exactly what Confirmation asks of every Christian, to carry Christ into ordinary places.
reflectionPrompts: Whom am I being asked to carry right now, and what makes that burden feel heavy?
Before my next trip, pray by name for the people traveling with me, and drive or ride with deliberate courtesy.
Read Matthew 11:25–30 in the Douay-Rheims and ask what it means that Christ's burden is light.

Another early martyr best known through a later legend

clare-of-assisi.heroSummary: St. Clare of Assisi is honored in Catholic tradition as a patron of television, embroiderers and goldsmiths. Inspired by Francis, she left her noble family in 1211 or 1212 and led the Poor Ladies at San Damiano for four decades, guarding their poverty. Her Rule was approved two days before her death in 1253; her feast is August 11.
clare-of-assisi.searchDescription: St. Clare of Assisi, feast August 11, followed Francis into poverty, led the Poor Ladies at San Damiano and saw her Rule approved in 1253.

symbols.meaning: Recalls the account, retold by Benedict XVI, that soldiers threatening San Damiano and Assisi were driven off after she prayed with the Blessed Sacrament. Art often shows a monstrance, which belongs to later tradition rather than her own time.
Her consecrated virginity; the Church keeps her day as the memorial of St. Clare, Virgin.
Her contemplation of Christ crucified, whom she urges Agnes of Prague in her letters to look upon and follow.
The plain dress of the Poor Ladies of San Damiano, the community of prayer and Gospel poverty she founded and led.

clare-of-assisi.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Clare when they want a steadier, more prayerful heart. She gave up wealth and the marriage expected of her, not to escape the world but to belong entirely to Christ, and she spent about forty years in one small monastery praying for the Church. Her letters to Agnes of Prague show a woman of warmth and joy, urging her friend to gaze on Christ as into a mirror. Catholics ask her help with prayer, with simplicity of life, and in sickness. Because, tradition holds, she saw the Christmas liturgy from her sickbed, Pius XII named her patron of television.

quotes.text: O sweet virgin, beloved in Christ, the joy of angels, and the crown of our sisters, place your mind in the mirror of eternity; place your soul in the figure of the Divine Substance, and in contemplating God transform yourself into an image of His Deity.
quotes.work: Third Letter to Agnes of Prague
quotes.translation: Charlotte Balfour, The Life and Legend of the Lady Saint Clare (London: Longmans, Green, 1910), public domain

quotes.text: What you have already, keep; what you have done, do still. Never stand still, but run swiftly, in steadfast imitation and with eager feet, lest in your progress you catch the dust.
quotes.work: Second Letter to Agnes of Prague
quotes.translation: Charlotte Balfour, The Life and Legend of the Lady Saint Clare (London: Longmans, Green, 1910), public domain

quotes.text: For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that being rich he became poor, for your sakes; that through his poverty you might be rich.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus Christ, you made yourself poor for our sake, and St. Clare loved your poverty with her whole heart. Through her prayers, free me from whatever clutters my heart and my days. Teach me to look at you as into a clear mirror, and to see there both your love and the person you call me to be. Give our families and communities her gift of mutual love and peace, and make our homes places of prayer. When I am sick or weary, let me rest in you as she did, until I see you face to face. Amen.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on August 11, the memorial of St. Clare, Virgin, in the General Roman Calendar.
Join a Transitus service on the evening of August 10, when many Poor Clare and Franciscan communities recall her death.
Ask a Poor Clare monastery near you to pray for an intention, and consider supporting the sisters, who live by their work and by alms.
Read one of her four letters to Agnes of Prague slowly, then spend a few quiet minutes before the Blessed Sacrament.
Pray for people who work in television and media, the patronage Pius XII gave her because of her Christmas vision.

clare-of-assisi.confirmationNote: Clare suits a confirmand drawn to prayer, simplicity, or a quiet kind of courage. As a young woman she made a costly decision, then stayed faithful to it for the rest of her life, defending her community's way of poverty with patience and persistence. Choosing her means asking the Holy Spirit for a heart fixed on Christ, and for the steadiness to keep a good commitment when it becomes hard.
reflectionPrompts: What is cluttering my heart and keeping me from looking at Christ clearly?
Spend ten minutes this week in silent prayer before the Blessed Sacrament, bringing nothing but my attention.
Read Clare's third letter to Agnes of Prague alongside 2 Corinthians 8:9 in the Douay-Rheims, and note what each says about poverty and riches.

claude-de-la-colombi-re.heroSummary: St. Claude La Colombière was a seventeenth-century French Jesuit, preacher and spiritual director. At Paray-le-Monial he became the confessor of St. Margaret Mary Alacoque, judged her experiences of the Sacred Heart to be genuine and helped spread that devotion. Imprisoned in London during the Popish Plot, he died at Paray in 1682. His feast is February 15.
claude-de-la-colombi-re.searchDescription: St. Claude La Colombière, feast February 15: French Jesuit, confessor of St. Margaret Mary and apostle of the Sacred Heart, known for trust in God.

symbols.meaning: He entered the Society of Jesus at seventeen and lived as a Jesuit teacher, preacher and director of souls. The chapel at Paray that holds his relics is served by Jesuits and honors him among other Jesuit saints.

He accepted Margaret Mary's account of Christ's Heart burning with love and became one of the first to make the devotion known. The great mosaic in his chapel at Paray shows him among the Jesuits who spread it.

A painting above his relics at Paray shows him saying Mass while Margaret Mary, receiving Communion, sees the Heart of Jesus joined with her heart and his. It pictures the spiritual friendship between confessor and penitent that she described.

A stained-glass window in his chapel recalls his arrest and weeks in King's Bench Prison after false accusations in the Popish Plot, an ordeal that broke his health before he was expelled from England.

claude-de-la-colombi-re.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Claude La Colombière when anxiety crowds out trust. He knew fear himself: his early notes admit a strong aversion to the religious life he was choosing, yet he gave himself to it completely. He listened carefully to a troubled young nun, St. Margaret Mary, and helped her believe that God was truly speaking to her. In London he served at court amid suspicion, then endured prison and exile with patience. His sermons and prayers return again and again to confidence in God's mercy. He is a gentle companion for anyone learning to hand the past, the future and their own weakness over to Christ.

quotes.text: Take up my yoke upon you, and learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart: and you shall find rest to your souls.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, you showed St. Claude La Colombière the love of your Sacred Heart and gave him the grace to trust you in every trial. Through his prayers, quiet my fears. I place my past in your mercy and my future in your love. When I fail, help me to begin again without discouragement; when I am misunderstood or treated unjustly, keep me patient and free of bitterness. Make me a faithful friend and a wise listener to those who struggle, as he was for St. Margaret Mary. Teach me to say from the heart that my hope is in you. Amen.
prayer.note: The longer "Act of Confidence" ("I am so convinced, my God, that you watch over all who hope in you…") is widely prayed in his name; EWTN notes that it is properly part of a sermon on the love of God. Its English wording varies between translations.

link.label: Act of Confidence (EWTN prayer library)

feastCustoms: February 15 is not a memorial in the universal Roman calendar, but the Roman Martyrology commemorates him that day and Jesuit communities honor him; the Sanctuary of the Sacred Heart at Paray-le-Monial marks it with a solemn Mass.
Pray the Act of Confidence slowly, naming one worry you want to place in God's hands.
Make a small act of devotion to the Sacred Heart, such as a short consecration or a visit to the Blessed Sacrament, in thanks for the devotion he helped spread.
If you visit Paray-le-Monial, pray at the Chapel of St. Claude La Colombière, where his relics are kept, and at the nearby Chapel of the Apparitions.
Read a few pages of his spiritual retreat notes or letters, or pray for priests who serve as confessors and spiritual directors.

claude-de-la-colombi-re.confirmationNote: Claude suits a confirmand who worries a great deal, wants to grow in trust, or hopes to be a good listener and friend. He was a Jesuit teacher who took a younger person's spiritual struggles seriously and helped her follow God's call. Confirmation strengthens Christians to bear witness under pressure, and his patience in prison and exile shows that trust in God can hold even when life goes badly.
reflectionPrompts: What part of my past am I still holding on to instead of leaving it to God's mercy?
This week, write down one fear, pray the Act of Confidence over it, and set it aside again each time it returns.
Read the Vatican's biography of St. Claude La Colombière, then read Matthew 11:28–30 in the Douay-Rheims and consider why devotion to the Sacred Heart draws on that passage.
