dominic-of-silos.heroSummary: St. Dominic of Silos is a patron of prisoners and captives and of expectant mothers. A former shepherd from Cañas, he became a Benedictine monk, refused a king's demand for monastery funds, and was sent to restore the ruined abbey of Silos in Castile. He died there on December 20, 1073.
dominic-of-silos.searchDescription: St. Dominic of Silos (c. 1000–1073), feast December 20: Benedictine abbot who restored Silos, patron of prisoners, captives and expectant mothers.

symbols.meaning: The prisoners and enslaved Christians whose freedom he is remembered for winning; he is often painted with freed captives in chains.

symbols.symbol: Abbot's crozier with a veil tied to it
symbols.meaning: His office as abbot of Silos; his staff was later carried to the bedside of Spanish queens in childbirth.
His authority as abbot; he is shown as a mitred abbot, sometimes enthroned.
The learning he fostered; the abbey's scriptorium became known for its manuscripts.

dominic-of-silos.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Dominic of Silos when someone they love is bound, whether in prison, in captivity, or in a hard pregnancy. He began life minding sheep, became a monk, and stood his ground when a king wanted the monastery's wealth for war, losing his post as a result. Given a ruined abbey instead, he patiently rebuilt it in stone and in spirit. Catholic sources remember him for helping to free Christian captives, and Spanish mothers have long asked his prayers for safe births. Tradition holds that Dominic de Guzmán's mother prayed at his tomb before her son was born.

quotes.text: The Lord looseth them that are fettered: The Lord enlighteneth the blind. The Lord lifteth up them that are cast down: the Lord loveth the just.
The Spirit of the Lord is upon me. Wherefore he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor, he hath sent me to heal the contrite of heart, To preach deliverance to the captives...

prayer.text: Lord God, you called St. Dominic of Silos from the sheepfold to the cloister and gave him courage to refuse what was wrong and patience to rebuild what was broken. Through his prayers, remember all who are imprisoned or held captive, and open the doors that keep them from freedom and from you. Watch over mothers who are expecting a child, and bring them and their babies safely through. Help me to be faithful in small beginnings and steady when I am treated unjustly. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: December 20 is his commemoration in the Roman Martyrology; he is not on the General Roman Calendar, so remember him in personal prayer on the anniversary of his death.
Pray for prisoners and their families, or support your parish or diocesan prison ministry.
Pray for an expectant mother you know, or for a safe birth for a family in your parish.
Listen to Gregorian chant sung by the monks of Silos, whose community still lives in the abbey he restored.
Read Luke 4:16–21 in the Douay-Rheims and ask where Christ is asking you to bring freedom to someone.

places.name: Abbey of Santo Domingo de Silos

dominic-of-silos.confirmationNote: Dominic of Silos suits a confirmand who wants courage to say no to pressure and patience to rebuild. He refused a king's demand to hand over what belonged to the monastery, lost his position, and then spent decades restoring a struggling community. Confirmation strengthens Christians to stand firm in faith, and his life shows that faithfulness can mean both resisting what is wrong and quietly building what is good.
reflectionPrompts: Who in my life is 'bound' by something, and how could I pray for or help them this week?
Find out whether your parish or diocese has a prison ministry, and offer one practical form of help.
Read the history page of the Abbey of Silos and Luke 4:16–21 in the Douay-Rheims, and note how the abbey's story reflects the restoration Christ announces.

dominic-savio.heroSummary: St. Dominic Savio is honored by the Salesians as a patron of young choir singers, and many expectant mothers ask his prayers. A pupil of St. John Bosco in Turin, he made holiness out of ordinary school life: prayer, study, friendship and cheerfulness. He died in 1857, not yet fifteen. The Salesian family celebrates him on May 6.
dominic-savio.searchDescription: St. Dominic Savio (1842–1857), feast May 6: John Bosco's pupil in Turin, who showed that holiness can mean cheerfulness and faithfulness in small things.
dominic-savio.whyWeTurn: People turn to Dominic Savio because he shows that holiness does not have to wait for adulthood. At seven he wrote four simple resolutions for his First Communion, and he kept rereading them. At Don Bosco's Oratory he learned that the way to God ran through cheerfulness, schoolwork and kindness rather than harsh penances. He taught catechism to younger boys, cared for sick companions and tried to settle fights. Students, altar servers and young people who want to take faith seriously see a friend in him, and many expectant mothers ask his prayers through the Salesian abitino devotion.

quotes.text: 1. I will go to Confession often, and as frequently to Holy Communion as my confessor allows. 2. I wish to sanctify the Sundays and festivals in a special manner. 3. My friends shall be Jesus and Mary. 4. Death rather than sin.
quotes.work: John Bosco, The Life of Dominic Savio, ch. on his First Communion resolutions (written by Dominic in 1849, aged seven)
quotes.translation: The Life of Dominic Savio, translated from the original work of John Bosco (London: Salesian Press, 1915; public domain)

quotes.text: Oh! what a beautiful sight I behold...
quotes.work: John Bosco, The Life of Dominic Savio (his last words, as reported by his father)
quotes.translation: The Life of Dominic Savio, translated from the original work of John Bosco (London: Salesian Press, 1915; public domain)

quotes.text: Sing joyfully to God, all the earth: serve ye the Lord with gladness.
quotes.work: Psalm 99:2 (the Latin 'Servite Domino in laetitia' was the motto Dominic gave a new companion, according to Bosco)

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, you drew St. Dominic Savio to yourself while he was still a schoolboy, and you made his ordinary days holy. Through his prayers, help me to choose you as my friend, to go often to confession and Communion, and to keep my promises to you. Teach me to serve you with gladness, in my studies, my work and my friendships. Watch over young people who are sick or struggling, and protect mothers who are expecting a child. Mary, Mother of God, keep me close to your Son. Amen.

feastCustoms: The Salesian family celebrates his feast on May 6; he is not on the General Roman Calendar, and March 9, the day he died, appears in some older calendars.
Write your own short list of resolutions, as he did for his First Communion, and keep it where you will reread it.
Pray for a young person who is ill, or for students facing exams.
Pray for expectant mothers you know; at the Basilica of Mary Help of Christians in Turin, the Salesians offer the 'abitino' of St. Dominic Savio in support of life.
Do one ordinary duty cheerfully today, as Bosco taught him.

places.name: Basilica of Mary Help of Christians (Valdocco)

dominic-savio.confirmationNote: Dominic Savio suits a confirmand who wants to take faith seriously now, not someday. He made firm resolutions at his First Communion, chose Jesus and Mary as his friends, and lived them out at school through prayer, study and kindness to others. Confirmation strengthens Christians to witness to Christ among their peers, and Dominic shows how that witness can be joyful, steady and very ordinary.
reflectionPrompts: Which of Dominic's four resolutions do I most need in my own life right now?
This week, help one person at school or work who is left out, struggling or in a quarrel, as Dominic tried to do.
Read the chapter on Dominic's First Communion resolutions in Bosco's Life of Dominic Savio (1915 Salesian Press translation, on the Internet Archive) and Psalm 99 in the Douay-Rheims.

dulce-lopes-pontes.heroSummary: St. Dulce Lopes Pontes, known as Sister Dulce or Santa Dulce dos Pobres, was a Brazilian religious sister from Salvador, Bahia. She cared for the sick and poor so persistently that a convent henhouse became the seed of a large hospital. She died in 1992, was canonized in 2019, and is remembered locally on August 13.
dulce-lopes-pontes.searchDescription: St. Dulce Lopes Pontes (1914–1992), Sister Dulce of Bahia: Brazilian nun whose care for the sick poor grew into a major charity. Remembered August 13.
dulce-lopes-pontes.whyWeTurn: People turn to Sister Dulce when the needs in front of them seem too big. She did not start with a plan or a budget. As a girl in Salvador she welcomed poor and sick people into her family's home, and as a sister she kept answering the next need: a clinic, a workers' association, a school, and finally a henhouse turned into shelter for the sick. She worked through years of serious lung illness. Vatican News recalls that she spoke of small acts of love that Jesus makes great. Nurses, volunteers and anyone serving the poor can ask her prayers for courage.

quotes.text: For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink; I was a stranger, and you took me in: Naked, and you covered me: sick, and you visited me...
Amen I say to you, as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, you lived in the sick, the hungry and the homeless whom St. Dulce welcomed in Salvador. Through her prayers, open my eyes to the people I would rather not see, and give me a heart that answers their need without waiting for perfect conditions. When I am tired or unwell, let me still offer small acts of love, trusting you to make them fruitful. Bless all who care for the sick and the poor, and strengthen those who suffer without help. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: August 13 is her liturgical memorial in Brazil, recalling the day in 1933 when she received the religious habit; she is not on the General Roman Calendar, so elsewhere remember her in personal prayer.
In Salvador, many devotees prepare with a trezena, thirteen days of prayer leading up to August 13, and visit her tomb at the Santuário Santa Dulce dos Pobres.
Visit someone who is sick, elderly or alone, remembering the people she welcomed into her home.
Give time or support to a hospital, clinic or charity that serves people who cannot pay.
Read Matthew 25:31–46 in the Douay-Rheims and choose one concrete work of mercy for the week.

places.name: Santuário Santa Dulce dos Pobres (Obras Sociais Irmã Dulce)

dulce-lopes-pontes.confirmationNote: Dulce suits a confirmand drawn to serving the sick, the poor or anyone overlooked. She began helping neighbors as a teenager, kept responding to each new need with whatever she had, and continued despite serious illness. Confirmation strengthens Christians to show Christ's love in deeds, and Sister Dulce shows how small, persistent acts of mercy can grow into lasting care for many people.
reflectionPrompts: Whose need have I noticed but avoided because I felt I could not do enough?
This week, do one concrete work of mercy, such as a visit, a meal or a donation, without waiting for ideal conditions.
Read Matthew 25:31–46 in the Douay-Rheims and the Vatican News biography of St. Dulce Lopes Pontes, and note how her work answers each need Jesus names.

dunstan.heroSummary: St. Dunstan is the patron saint of goldsmiths, a craft he practised himself. A tenth-century monk, he rebuilt Glastonbury Abbey, became archbishop of Canterbury, and helped renew monastic life across England. He also made bells and played the harp. He died at Canterbury in 988, and his feast is May 19.
dunstan.searchDescription: St. Dunstan (d. 988), feast May 19: abbot of Glastonbury and archbishop of Canterbury, monastic reformer, metalworker and patron of goldsmiths.

symbols.meaning: His real skill as a metalworker; tradition adds the late legend that he seized the devil by the nose with his tongs, which is not part of his documented life.
The inspiration of the Holy Spirit; older images show a dove near him or at his ear as he stands at the altar.
The angels who, according to his early biographers, warned him of his approaching death.
His love of music; the Catholic Encyclopedia notes that he played the harp in his cell.

symbols.symbol: Kneeling at the feet of Christ
symbols.meaning: His humility before God; a drawing of a monk prostrate before Christ, long believed to be his own work, survives from Glastonbury.

dunstan.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Dunstan when their work is done with their hands. He was a scholar and a church leader, but he also worked metal, made bells and organs, and played the harp, and medieval goldsmiths took him as their patron. His life was not quiet: he was driven into exile, returned, and spent decades working with kings and fellow bishops to renew prayer and learning in England. Tradition adds the story of the devil and the tongs, which is legend. Craftspeople, musicians, and anyone whose faith must live alongside public responsibility can find in him a steady companion.

quotes.text: He hath made a remembrance of his wonderful works, being a merciful and gracious Lord: He hath given food to them that fear him.
quotes.work: Psalm 110:4–5 (the verses the Catholic Encyclopedia records as his last words)

prayer.text: Lord God, you gave St. Dunstan skilful hands, a love of learning, and the courage to renew your Church. Through his prayers, bless the work of my hands and help me do it honestly and well, for your glory and not my own. Make my life a song of praise, as his music was. When I face opposition or must start again, give me patience and a steady heart. Keep me humble at the feet of your Son, and at the end of my days let me give thanks for your wonderful works. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: In England, May 19 is the optional memorial of St. Dunstan, Bishop; elsewhere he is commemorated in the Roman Martyrology, so remember him in personal prayer.
Pray Psalm 110 (Psalm 111 in modern numbering), the psalm whose words he spoke as he died.
Pray for goldsmiths, metalworkers, jewellers and all craftspeople, or thank someone whose handiwork you use every day.
Make or mend something by hand, or play or sing a piece of sacred music, as an offering to God.
If you visit Canterbury or Glastonbury, pray at the places where he lived, worked and was buried.

places.name: Glastonbury Abbey

dunstan.confirmationNote: Dunstan suits a confirmand who loves making things, music or study, or who expects to carry responsibility in public life. He worked as a craftsman and musician, led a monastery, and served as archbishop through exile and political conflict without abandoning prayer. Confirmation strengthens Christians to witness to Christ in every part of life, and Dunstan shows that skilled work and leadership can both be offered to God.
reflectionPrompts: What work of my hands, mind or voice could I offer more consciously to God?
This week, do one practical task slowly and carefully, as an act of prayer rather than a chore to rush through.
Read the Catholic Encyclopedia article on St. Dunstan and Psalm 110 in the Douay-Rheims, and note what his last words say about how he understood his life.

dymphna.heroSummary: St. Dymphna is honored as a patron of people living with mental illness and of those who care for them. Her story comes from a thirteenth-century legend about an Irish princess killed at Geel, in present-day Belgium. Her best-documented legacy is Geel itself, where families have welcomed people with mental illness into their homes for centuries.
dymphna.searchDescription: St. Dymphna, feast May 15: the legend of an Irish princess martyred at Geel, Belgium, and her patronage of people living with mental illness.

symbols.meaning: The instrument of her death in the legend, which says her father beheaded her when she refused him. The Catholic Encyclopedia and Vatican News both name the sword as her attribute.

Older images show her holding a fettered devil or standing over a small demon, a sign that she is invoked as a protector against evil. It speaks of spiritual protection; it is not a statement about people who live with mental illness.
She is pictured as a princess because tradition makes her the daughter of an Irish king. Catholic Culture's list of her representations includes a princess holding a lamp and a sword.
Sometimes placed in her hands, recalling the Christian faith that, according to the legend, she kept in spite of her father's paganism and his threats.

dymphna.whyWeTurn: People living with depression, anxiety or other mental illness, and the families and caregivers who walk beside them, often turn to St. Dymphna. Her life reaches us only as legend, but tradition holds that she was a young woman who fled a parent's abuse and kept her faith. What is clearer is what her shrine inspired: in Geel, ordinary families learned to open their homes to people others avoided. Asking her prayers is never a substitute for medical care or counseling. It is a way to ask for courage, patience and good companions, and to remember that no one is beyond God's tenderness.

quotes.text: Come to me, all you that labour, and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take up my yoke upon you, and learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart: and you shall find rest to your souls.
Amen I say to you, as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, you invite all who labor and are burdened to come to you and find rest. Through the prayers of St. Dymphna, stay close to everyone who struggles with mental illness, especially those who feel alone, ashamed or afraid. Give them skilled doctors, wise counselors and faithful friends, and the courage to ask for help. Strengthen the families and caregivers who stay beside them. Make our homes and parishes places of welcome, as Geel became, so that no one is treated as a burden or a stranger. Amen.

link.label: National Shrine of St. Dymphna: Novena in Honor of St. Dymphna

feastCustoms: Remember her on May 15, the day kept at Geel and at the National Shrine of St. Dymphna in Massillon, Ohio. She is not on the General Roman Calendar, and the current Roman Martyrology, as given by Vatican News and Catholic Culture, lists her on May 30.
Pray for someone you know who is struggling with their mental health, then reach out with a message or a visit. If anyone is in immediate danger, contact local emergency services first.
Pray the U.S. bishops' Novena for Mental Health, which turns to St. Dymphna on its first day and ends on the feast of St. Luke, October 18.
In Geel, a costumed Sint-Dimpna Ommegang retelling her legend and the town's history is held once every five years.
Learn about Geel's tradition of family care, in which local households take in people with mental illness, and ask what your own parish does to welcome them.

dymphna.confirmationNote: Dymphna is a fitting name for a confirmand who has known family pain, who lives with anxiety or depression, or who wants to stand beside people who do. Her life comes to us as legend, but the faith it describes is brave and clear, and the town that honors her shows what Christian welcome looks like. Choosing her name can be a promise to treat every struggling person with dignity and patience.
reflectionPrompts: Who in my life might be carrying a hidden struggle with anxiety, depression or grief, and how could I let them know they are not alone?
This week, check in on one friend or family member, and find out what mental-health support your parish, school or diocese offers.
Read Matthew 25:31–46, then the Catholic Encyclopedia's article on St. Dymphna, and notice how it separates her legend from the history of care at Geel.

edith-stein.heroSummary: St. Teresa Benedicta of the Cross, born Edith Stein, is a patron of Europe, one of three women John Paul II named co-patronesses of the continent in 1999. A Jewish-born philosopher who became a Catholic and a Discalced Carmelite nun, she was murdered at Auschwitz in 1942. Catholics remember her on August 9.
edith-stein.searchDescription: St. Teresa Benedicta of the Cross (Edith Stein): Jewish-born philosopher, Carmelite nun and patron of Europe, killed at Auschwitz in 1942. Feast: August 9.

symbols.meaning: Her religious life as Sister Teresa Benedicta, which began at the Cologne Carmel in 1933 and continued at Echt in the Netherlands.
Her religious name, which the Holy See renders "blessed of the Cross," and her last major work, The Science of the Cross, on St. John of the Cross.
Her Jewish birth and family, and the Nazi persecution of people of Jewish ancestry in which she and her sister Rosa died; Catholic Culture lists it as her symbol.
Her work as a philosopher, teacher and writer, and her lifelong search for truth; in the Edith Stein Society's icon the book is labeled "Veritas."

edith-stein.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Teresa Benedicta because she held together things others thought could not meet: a demanding mind and a deep faith, love for her Jewish family and a Catholic vocation. She searched for truth through philosophy until reading St. Teresa of Avila's life convinced her she had found it. Students, teachers, converts, and anyone wrestling with hard questions find in her a companion who took both reason and prayer seriously. She also accompanies people who grieve the Holocaust and those working for understanding between Christians and Jews. Her last recorded words to her sister Rosa, "Come, we are going for our people," show a love that did not turn away from suffering.

quotes.text: But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ; by whom the world is crucified to me, and I to the world.
Jesus saith to him: I am the way, and the truth, and the life.

prayer.text: God of truth, you led Saint Teresa Benedicta of the Cross through long searching to your Son, and you gave her courage to share the suffering of her people. Through her prayers, give me an honest mind that keeps asking until it finds you, and a heart that loves without conditions. Comfort all who suffer because of hatred for who they are, and heal the wounds between Christians and Jews. Teach me to accept the crosses of each day, trusting that your love is stronger than death. Amen.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on August 9, her optional memorial in the General Roman Calendar and the date commonly given for her death at Auschwitz.
Pray for understanding between Christians and Jews and for all victims of the Holocaust, themes John Paul II stressed when he named her a co-patron of Europe.
Read part of her own writing, such as Life in a Jewish Family or her essays on women, as Catholic Culture suggests for her day.
Offer a small sacrifice and reflect on the everyday crosses you carry, recalling the meaning of her religious name.
Learn about Auschwitz, where both she and St. Maximilian Kolbe died, through the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum.

edith-stein.confirmationNote: St. Teresa Benedicta of the Cross can suit a Confirmation candidate who loves hard questions. She studied philosophy at a high level, searched honestly for truth, and found it in Christ without ever disowning her Jewish family. Taking her name can mean committing to think carefully, pray seriously, stand against prejudice, and accept the crosses that come with faithfulness.
reflectionPrompts: What question about God or faith are you carrying right now, and who could you talk it through with honestly?
Visit a Holocaust memorial or museum, in person or online, and pray for the people whose stories you meet there.

Read the Holy See's biography of Edith Stein, then John Paul II's 1999 apostolic letter naming her a co-patroness of Europe, and note why he saw her as a bridge between her Jewish roots and her Christian faith.

edmund-campion.heroSummary: St. Edmund Campion was a gifted Oxford scholar who became a Jesuit and returned to Elizabethan England in 1580 to serve Catholics in secret. Captured, racked and tried for treason, he insisted that his mission was religious, not political. He was executed at Tyburn on December 1, 1581, and canonized in 1970 among the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales.
edmund-campion.searchDescription: St. Edmund Campion, feast December 1: Oxford scholar turned Jesuit priest, author of the famous "Brag," martyred at Tyburn in 1581.
edmund-campion.whyWeTurn: Catholics turn to St. Edmund Campion when faith asks for courage and clear thinking at the same time. He gave up a promising career at Oxford, became a Jesuit, and came home to a country where saying Mass could cost a priest his life. He moved quietly between households to bring the sacraments, yet he also wrote openly, asking for a fair hearing and offering to debate the learned. Under torture and at his trial he held to what he had said from the start: he came to save souls, not to plot. Students, teachers and anyone defending the faith in a hostile setting ask his prayers for courage joined to charity.

quotes.text: My charge is, of free cost to preach the Gospel, to minister the sacraments, to instruct the simple, to reform sinners, to confute errors, and, in brief, to cry alarm spiritual against foul vice and proud ignorance, wherewith many my dear countrymen are abused.
quotes.work: Letter to the Lords of the Privy Council ("Campion's Brag"), 1580, article 3
quotes.translation: Written in English; text as printed in Richard Simpson, Edmund Campion: A Biography (1867), p. 159 (public domain)

quotes.text: The expense is reckoned, the enterprise is begun; it is of God, it cannot be withstood. So the faith was planted, so it must be restored.
quotes.work: Letter to the Lords of the Privy Council ("Campion's Brag"), 1580, article 8
quotes.translation: Written in English; text as printed in Richard Simpson, Edmund Campion: A Biography (1867), p. 161 (public domain)

quotes.text: I have no more to say, but to recommend your case and mine to Almighty God, the Searcher of hearts, who send us of His grace, and set us at accord before the day of payment, to the intent we may at last be friends in heaven, where all injuries shall be forgotten.
quotes.work: Letter to the Lords of the Privy Council ("Campion's Brag"), 1580, article 9
quotes.translation: Written in English; text as printed in Richard Simpson, Edmund Campion: A Biography (1867), p. 161 (public domain)

prayer.text: Lord Jesus Christ, you gave St. Edmund Campion a brilliant mind and a brave heart, and he spent both in your service. Through his prayers, give me the courage to speak the truth with charity and the humility to listen well to those who disagree with me. Strengthen everyone who suffers for their faith today, and keep me faithful in small trials as well as great ones. Help me to count the cost of following you and still say yes. May we all at last be friends in heaven, where every injury is forgotten. Amen.

feastCustoms: Remember him on December 1, the anniversary of his death at Tyburn. Jesuit communities and schools keep the day, which the Jesuits in Britain call Campion Day.
In England, the English Martyrs are celebrated together on May 4, a feast in the national calendar honoring the men and women martyred for the Catholic faith between 1535 and 1680.
At Stonyhurst College, a relic of the rope that bound him to the hurdle on his way to Tyburn is placed on the altar each December 1.
Pray at the Martyrs' Shrine of Tyburn Convent in London, near the site of the Tyburn gallows, where relics of the Tyburn martyrs are kept.

edmund-rich.heroSummary: St. Edmund of Abingdon, also called Edmund Rich, taught at Oxford and Paris before becoming Archbishop of Canterbury in 1234. He pressed for church reform, clashed with Henry III and withdrew to the Cistercian abbey of Pontigny in France. He died at Soisy in 1240, was buried at Pontigny and was soon canonized.
edmund-rich.searchDescription: St. Edmund of Abingdon (Edmund Rich), feast November 16: Oxford teacher, reforming Archbishop of Canterbury and spiritual writer buried at Pontigny.
edmund-rich.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Edmund of Abingdon as a scholar who never let learning crowd out prayer. Tradition remembers a teacher who gave away his income to the poor, kept a strict personal discipline and was gentle with the sick. As archbishop he tried to reform the Church and keep peace in a divided kingdom, and he did not always succeed; his last months were spent in exile. His Mirror of Holy Church teaches ordinary believers to see God's goodness in creation, in Scripture and in prayer. Students, teachers and anyone carrying responsibility through conflict ask his prayers for wisdom and a peaceful heart.

quotes.text: To live perfectly, as St Bernard teaches us, is to live honourably, meekly and charitably.

quotes.text: …care not if thou multiply not many Paters, for it is better to say one Pater noster with good devotion.

prayer.text: Lord God, you gave St. Edmund a love of learning and a deeper love for you. Through his prayers, help me to study honestly and to pray with my heart, not only with my lips. Teach me to see your goodness in creation, in Scripture and in the people around me. When I carry responsibility, make me fair and brave; when conflict wears me down, give me peace and keep me from bitterness. Bless all students and teachers, and help us to live honourably, meekly and charitably. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: Remember him on November 16, the day of his death. The national calendar for England lists him that day; he is not on the General Roman Calendar.

Pray one Our Father slowly, phrase by phrase, following his advice in the Mirror that one Pater noster said with devotion is better than many said without it.
In England, the Diocese of Portsmouth honors him as its patron, and St Edmund's College, Ware, which was placed under his patronage in 1793, began its studies on his feast.
Pilgrims still visit the former Cistercian abbey church at Pontigny in Burgundy, where his body is venerated.

edward-the-confessor.heroSummary: St. Edward the Confessor was king of England from 1042 until his death in January 1066. Raised in exile in Normandy, he ruled through a largely peaceful reign, gave generously to the poor, and rebuilt Westminster Abbey, where his shrine remains. Canonized in 1161, he is honored on October 13.
edward-the-confessor.searchDescription: St. Edward the Confessor (about 1003–1066), king of England who rebuilt Westminster Abbey and was known for almsgiving. Feast October 13.

symbols.symbol: Crown and sceptre, sometimes topped with a dove
symbols.meaning: His office as king of England; the Catholic Encyclopedia describes his reign as one of almost unbroken peace, and Westminster Abbey records that a crown, sceptre and ring were found with his body when his tomb was opened in 1102.

symbols.symbol: Ring held up or given to a beggar
symbols.meaning: Tradition holds that he gave his ring to a poor man who was St. John the Evangelist in disguise, and that the ring was later returned to him with word that his death was near.
His almsgiving; he was remembered for giving freely to the sick and poor at the palace gate.

symbols.symbol: Carrying a sick man or curing the sick
symbols.meaning: The healings associated with him; the Catholic Encyclopedia calls him the first English king to touch for the "king's evil" (scrofula).
His devotion to St. John the Evangelist, his favorite saint, in whose name he would refuse no request.

edward-the-confessor.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Edward because he held real power and tried to use it gently. Exile taught him early how fragile ambition is, and as king he avoided needless wars, lifted a hated tax, and gave so freely that later generations looked back to "the good St. Edward's laws." He loved the liturgy and kept a promise to honor St. Peter by rebuilding the abbey at Westminster. Tradition holds that he gave his own ring to a beggar who turned out to be St. John. Catholics ask his prayers for leaders, for generosity to the poor, and for marriages under strain.

quotes.text: He that hath the substance of this world, and shall see his brother in need, and shall shut up his bowels from him: how doth the charity of God abide in him? My little children, let us not love in word, nor in tongue, but in deed, and in truth.
For he shall deliver the poor from the mighty: and the needy that had no helper. He shall spare the poor and needy: and he shall save the souls of the poor.

prayer.text: Lord God, you called St. Edward to rule a kingdom with gentleness and to open his hands to the poor. Through his prayers, teach me to hold whatever authority I have as a trust from you, and to choose peace over pride. Make me generous when someone asks for help, quick to share what I have, and attentive to the sick and forgotten. Strengthen husbands and wives whose marriages are strained, and guide all who lead nations and communities. Like St. Edward, may I love your house and long for the kingdom where you reign forever. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: In England, October 13, the anniversary of the translation of his relics in 1163, is an optional memorial in the National Calendar; the Roman Martyrology commemorates him on January 5, the day he died.
Give alms or practical help to someone who asks you, recalling the tradition of the ring he gave to a beggar.
Pray Psalm 71 (Psalm 72 in modern numbering) for all who govern, that they may defend the poor and needy.
Visit or pray for someone who is sick, remembering the healings associated with him.
At Westminster Abbey, now an Anglican church, the octave of St. Edward beginning October 13 includes an annual pilgrimage to the shrine where his body still rests.

edward-the-confessor.confirmationNote: Edward suits a confirmand who expects to lead others or who wants to grow in generosity. He spent years in exile, then used royal power with restraint, avoided needless wars and gave freely to the poor and sick. He also loved the Mass and built a great church in honor of St. Peter. Choosing his name can mean asking the Holy Spirit to make authority a form of service and wealth a means of charity.

egwin.heroSummary: St. Egwin was the third bishop of Worcester and the founder of Evesham Abbey, dedicated to the Virgin Mary, in the early eighth century. A Mercian of royal blood, he faced bitter opposition for his strict reforms and sought vindication in Rome. He died about 717 and is usually remembered on December 30.
egwin.searchDescription: St. Egwin (d. about 717), third bishop of Worcester and founder of Evesham Abbey, known for the legend of the fetters and the key. Feast December 30.

symbols.symbol: Fish with a key in its mouth
symbols.meaning: Tradition holds that the key to his fetters, thrown into the River Avon, was found in a fish caught in the Tiber while he prayed in Rome; it stands for God's vindication of the falsely accused.
The legend that he chained himself before his pilgrimage to Rome as an act of penance while he was under accusation.

symbols.symbol: Key and fetter-bolt in his hand
symbols.meaning: His release from those bonds, which the story links to his release from the charges brought against him.
His office as bishop of Worcester, which he accepted reluctantly and used to press for Christian discipline in a young Church.

egwin.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Egwin when they are misunderstood or accused. As bishop he insisted on Christian marriage and clerical discipline, and the resentment that followed sent him to Rome to clear his name. Tradition adds that he went in chains as penance and that the key came back to him in a fish; whatever the details, the story is about trusting God for vindication. He also listened when a herdsman reported a vision of Our Lady and built a monastery in her honor at Evesham. He is a companion for those carrying unfair blame, and for anyone who hopes to build something lasting for God.

quotes.text: O Lord, for I am thy servant: I am thy servant, and the son of thy handmaid. Thou hast broken my bonds: I will sacrifice to thee the sacrifice of praise, and I will call upon the name of the Lord.

prayer.text: Lord God, you gave St. Egwin the courage to call your people to holiness and the patience to bear accusation without bitterness. Through his prayers, help me to tell the truth even when it makes me unpopular, and to place my good name in your hands when others misjudge me. Loosen whatever binds me, whether sin, fear or resentment, and let me answer your mercy with praise. As he built a house of prayer in honor of the Virgin Mary, help me to build my life on faith that lasts. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: Remember him on December 30, his usual commemoration; he is not on the General Roman Calendar, and many older English martyrologies kept January 11, the date of a translation of his relics.
Pray for someone who has been falsely accused or whose reputation has been damaged, and for the courage to defend them.
Make a good Confession or take on a small act of penance, recalling the fetters he wore on the road to Rome.
Honor Our Lady, to whom he dedicated Evesham Abbey, by praying the Rosary or the Angelus.
In Evesham, the Catholic church of St. Mary and St. Egwin keeps the dedication of his abbey; the abbey's bell tower and parts of its precinct still stand in the town.

egwin.confirmationNote: Egwin suits a confirmand who cares about doing what is right even when it costs popularity. He accepted a responsibility he did not seek, called his people to live their faith seriously, and faced hostility for it. Rather than give up, he took his case to the Church and trusted God with the outcome. He also built a lasting place of prayer in honor of Mary, showing that courage and devotion belong together.

el-bieta-hesselblad.heroSummary: St. Mary Elizabeth Hesselblad was a Swedish nurse who became a Catholic in 1902 and, from St. Bridget's house in Rome, renewed the Bridgettine order in 1911. She worked for Christian unity, sheltered persecuted Jews during the Second World War, died in 1957, and was canonized in 2016. Her memorial is June 4.
el-bieta-hesselblad.searchDescription: St. Mary Elizabeth Hesselblad (1870–1957), Swedish nurse and convert who renewed the Bridgettine order in Rome. Canonized 2016; memorial June 4.
el-bieta-hesselblad.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Mary Elizabeth Hesselblad because her faith grew out of searching. Raised a Lutheran in a poor Swedish family, she went to America to earn a living, nursed the sick in their homes, and came to the Catholic Church through prayer, study and the witness of Catholic patients. In Rome she gave her fragile health to renewing St. Bridget's order and to praying for the unity of Christians. During the war her house became a refuge for people persecuted under the racial laws. Converts, nurses, anyone longing for Christian unity, and those who must trust God without seeing the path all find a companion in her.

quotes.text: That they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee; that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that thou hast sent me.
I was a stranger, and you took me in: Naked, and you covered me: sick, and you visited me.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus Christ, you led St. Mary Elizabeth through poverty, illness and long searching into the fullness of your Church. Through her prayers, give me a heart that keeps seeking the truth and follows it with courage. Make me gentle with the sick, welcoming to strangers and brave in protecting those who are persecuted. Heal the divisions among Christians, that all may be one as you and the Father are one. When I cannot see the way ahead, help me to hold your hand and trust you. Amen.

eleutherius.heroSummary: St. Eleutherius (also written Eleutherus) was bishop of Rome in the later second century. Hegesippus remembered him as a deacon under Pope Anicetus, and Irenaeus named him the twelfth bishop of Rome after the apostles. Imprisoned Christians of Lyon sent him a letter by Irenaeus. The Roman Martyrology remembers him on May 26.
eleutherius.searchDescription: St. Eleutherius, second-century bishop of Rome, received a letter from the imprisoned Christians of Lyon, carried by Irenaeus. Remembered May 26.
eleutherius.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Eleutherius as a quiet witness to how the early churches stayed connected. Almost everything we know about him comes from a few lines in Hegesippus, Irenaeus and Eusebius: he served as a deacon, became bishop of Rome, and received a letter from Christians in prison at Lyon, who asked him to welcome their messenger Irenaeus. Later stories about decrees and a British king are doubtful, and his martyrdom is not documented. What remains is enough: a pastor whom suffering Christians far away trusted. He is a fitting companion when we pray for the Pope, for persecuted believers, and for unity among local churches.

quotes.text: We pray, father Eleutherus, that you may rejoice in God in all things and always.
quotes.work: Letter of the martyrs of Lyon to Eleutherius, quoted in Eusebius, Church History, Book V, chapter 4, §2
quotes.translation: Arthur Cushman McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 1 (1890; public domain)

quotes.text: Soter succeeded Anicetus; and now, in the twelfth place from the apostles, Eleutherus holds the office of bishop.
quotes.work: Irenaeus, Against Heresies III.3.3, quoted in Eusebius, Church History, Book V, chapter 6, §4
quotes.translation: Arthur Cushman McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 1 (1890; public domain)

quotes.text: Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking care of it, not by constraint, but willingly, according to God: not for filthy lucre's sake, but voluntarily: Neither as lording it over the clergy, but being made a pattern of the flock from the heart.
quotes.work: 1 Peter 5:2–3, chosen for context; it is not about Eleutherius

prayer.text: Lord God, when Christians in prison at Lyon wrote to St. Eleutherius, they trusted him to hear them and to care for the peace of your Church. Through his prayers, bless our Pope and our bishops with patience and wisdom. Strengthen all who suffer for their faith, and let them know they are not forgotten. Teach me to listen carefully before I judge, to welcome those who are sent to me, and to treasure the bonds that join Christians in every place. Keep your Church one in truth and in love. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: Remember him on May 26, the date under which the Roman Martyrology commemorates him. He is not on the General Roman Calendar, and the Mass that day is usually the memorial of St. Philip Neri, so this is a day for personal or family prayer.
Read Eusebius, Church History, Book V, chapters 1–4, at New Advent: the letter of the Christians of Vienne and Lyon, and their note to Eleutherius commending Irenaeus.
Pray for the Pope by name, and for unity and peace among local churches.
Pray for Christians who are imprisoned or persecuted for their faith, as the martyrs of Lyon were when they wrote to him.
Write a short note of encouragement to a priest, missionary or friend far away, as a small sign that distance need not divide believers.
eleutherius.confirmationNote: Eleutherius suits a confirmand who values steady service more than the spotlight. He began as a deacon, helping his bishop, and later bore responsibility for the Church of Rome while Christians elsewhere were suffering and arguing over claims about prophecy. Little else about him is certain. Choosing him is a way of promising to stay connected to the wider Church and to support those who suffer for their faith.
reflectionPrompts: Who in my life is carrying a heavy burden far from me, and how can I let them know they are remembered?
This week, pray once for the Pope and your bishop by name, and once for Christians who are persecuted.
Read Eusebius, Church History, Book V, chapters 1–4, and note what the Christians of Lyon asked of Eleutherius and why they trusted Irenaeus.

elias-of-the-carmelites.heroSummary: Elijah (Elias) is the Old Testament prophet who challenged the worship of Baal on Mount Carmel, heard God in a gentle breeze at Horeb, and was taken up in a fiery chariot. Carmelites honor him as their spiritual father and model, and keep his feast on July 20, when the Roman Martyrology also commemorates him.
elias-of-the-carmelites.searchDescription: Elijah the Prophet, who faced the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel and heard God's quiet voice at Horeb, is honored by Carmelites on July 20.

symbols.meaning: Scripture says a fiery chariot parted him from Elisha and he went up to heaven by a whirlwind (4 Kings 2:11); icons of Elijah often show this ascent.
During the drought God sent ravens to feed him by the torrent of Carith (3 Kings 17:6), a sign of trust in God's provision; the scene appears in Elijah icons.

On the Carmelite shield, the arm and fiery sword of Elijah express his burning zeal for the one true God, with his words "Zelo zelatus sum" on a banner; Carmelites link it to the Word of God as the sword of the Spirit.
Elijah struck the Jordan with his mantle, and it passed to Elisha when Elijah was taken up (4 Kings 2:8–14), a sign of a calling handed on to a successor.

elias-of-the-carmelites.whyWeTurn: People turn to Elijah because his story holds both fire and weakness. He stood almost alone against the worship of Baal and the injustice of a king, yet he also ran for his life, sat under a tree and asked to die. God fed him, sent him on, and spoke to him not in wind or fire but in a gentle breeze. That makes him a companion for anyone who is worn out from doing right, and for anyone learning to pray in silence. Carmelites see in him the joining of prayer and responsibility for others. Tradition holds him as their father; history places their beginnings with medieval hermits who took him as their model.

quotes.text: How long do you halt between two sides? if the Lord be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him.
With zeal have I been zealous for the Lord God of hosts
quotes.work: 3 Kings (1 Kings) 19:10; the motto on the Carmelite shield

quotes.text: And after the earthquake a fire: the Lord is not in the fire, and after the fire a whistling of a gentle air.

prayer.text: Lord God of Elijah, your prophet stood firm on Mount Carmel and then, tired and afraid, fled into the wilderness, where you fed him and called him on. Through his prayers, give me courage to choose you without halting between two sides, and humility to accept help when I am worn out. Quiet the noise in me, so that I can hear you in the gentle breeze. Let my prayer make me more just and more caring toward others, as it did for him. Bless the Carmelite family and all who seek your face in silence. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: In Carmelite churches and communities, July 20 is kept as a solemnity of St. Elijah; the Irish Carmelites note they are the only group in the Western Church to keep this observance.
Elsewhere, remember him on July 20, when the Roman Martyrology commemorates him; Eastern Christians also honor him on this date.
Read his story in 3 Kings (1 Kings) 17–19 and 4 Kings (2 Kings) 2, perhaps one episode a day in the week before the feast.
Spend some time in silent prayer, as Elijah heard God in the gentle breeze rather than the wind, earthquake or fire.
Do something concrete for someone who is hungry or treated unjustly, remembering the widow of Sarephta and Naboth's vineyard.

elias-of-the-carmelites.confirmationNote: Elijah, or Elias, suits a confirmand who wants courage and a real life of prayer. He spoke up for God and for people wronged by the powerful, yet he also knew exhaustion and fear, and God met him there. Choosing him is a way of asking the Holy Spirit for zeal that stays humble and for the patience to listen in silence before acting.
reflectionPrompts: Where am I "halting between two sides" in my life, and what would it mean to choose God clearly?
Set aside ten minutes this week for silent prayer with no phone or music, listening for God as Elijah did at Horeb.
Read 3 Kings (1 Kings) 19 and 4 Kings (2 Kings) 2, then the Irish Carmelites' page on Elijah, and note how Carmelites connect his story to their way of prayer.

elizabeth-ann-seton.heroSummary: St. Elizabeth Ann Seton is honored as patron of Catholic schools. A New York wife, mother and young widow, she became Catholic in 1805, opened a school in Maryland and founded the Sisters of Charity of St. Joseph's at Emmitsburg. Canonized in 1975 as the first U.S.-born saint, she is remembered on January 4.
elizabeth-ann-seton.searchDescription: St. Elizabeth Ann Seton, wife, mother, widow and convert, founded the Sisters of Charity at Emmitsburg and was the first U.S.-born saint. Feast: January 4.
elizabeth-ann-seton.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Elizabeth Ann Seton because her holiness grew inside an ordinary, often painful family life. She was a wife and mother of five, lost her husband to tuberculosis far from home, faced her family's disapproval when she became Catholic, and later buried two daughters. Through all of it she kept seeking God's will in daily tasks and found deep joy in the Eucharist. Parents, widows, converts, teachers and anyone grieving find in her a companion who knew both loss and hope. She is especially remembered by Catholic schools, which see in her school at Emmitsburg part of their own beginnings.

quotes.text: At last, Amabilia, at last, God is mine and I am His. Now let all earthly things go as they will. I have received Him.
quotes.work: Letter to Amabilia Filicchi after her First Communion, March 25, 1805, in Memoir, Letters and Journal of Elizabeth Seton, ed. Robert Seton, vol. 1, p. 216

quotes.text: the first end I propose in our daily work is to do the will of God; secondly, to do it in the manner he wills it; and thirdly, to do it because it is his will.
quotes.work: Instruction to her sisters, in Charles I. White, Life of Mrs. Eliza A. Seton, p. 322

quotes.text: Be children of the Church; be children of the Church
quotes.work: Spoken to her sisters as she received the last anointing, January 1821, recorded in Charles I. White, Life of Mrs. Eliza A. Seton, p. 425

prayer.text: Lord God, you led St. Elizabeth Ann Seton through marriage, motherhood, grief and conversion, and made her a mother to many in her community and her schools. Through her prayers, help me to seek your will in my daily work and to do it gladly, in the way you want and because you want it. Comfort widows, grieving parents and all who feel alone in their faith. Bless Catholic schools, their teachers and their students, and make them places where children come to know and love you. Draw me closer to you in the Eucharist, as you drew her. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
prayer.note: The phrase about doing God's will in the way he wants and because he wants it paraphrases her instruction quoted above.

link.label: Prayers and quotes of St. Elizabeth Ann Seton (National Shrine)

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on January 4, her memorial in the dioceses of the United States (and Canada), which falls during the Christmas season; when January 4 is a Sunday, the Sunday liturgy takes its place.
Visit the Basilica of the National Shrine in Emmitsburg, Maryland, where her remains are entombed beneath the Altar of Relics, or pray along with the shrine online.
Meditate on her teaching that the first rule of daily work is to do God's will, and offer one ordinary task of the day with that intention.
Thank, pray for or support the teachers and students of a Catholic school.
Reach out to a widow, a grieving parent or someone recently received into the Church.

elizabeth-ann-seton.confirmationNote: Elizabeth Ann Seton suits a confirmand whose faith has been tested by loss or by standing apart from family and friends. She chose to become Catholic at real cost, then poured that faith into teaching children and building a community. She found God less in grand gestures than in doing his will in ordinary work. Choosing her is a way of asking for courage, steadiness and love for the Eucharist.
reflectionPrompts: What loss or disappointment in my life might God still be using to lead me somewhere new?
Choose one routine task this week and do it carefully, without rushing or dragging, as an offering to God.
Read her letter to Amabilia Filicchi of March 25, 1805, in the 1869 Memoir, Letters and Journal of Elizabeth Seton, and the shrine's biography, and note what drew her to the Eucharist.

elizabeth-mother-of-john-baptist.heroSummary: St. Elizabeth, mother of John the Baptist, is honored as patron of expectant mothers. Luke's Gospel calls her and her husband Zechariah righteous and long childless. When the pregnant Mary visited her, Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, greeted her as the mother of her Lord. She is traditionally remembered on November 5.
elizabeth-mother-of-john-baptist.searchDescription: St. Elizabeth, mother of John the Baptist and kinswoman of Mary, greeted Mary at the Visitation as the mother of her Lord. Patron of expectant mothers.

symbols.symbol: An older woman holding the infant John
symbols.meaning: Her son John the Baptist, born when she and Zechariah were advanced in years (Luke 1:7, 57).

symbols.symbol: Embracing the Virgin Mary, both expecting
symbols.meaning: The Visitation (Luke 1:39–45), when the child leaped in her womb and she blessed Mary and the fruit of her womb.
The priest Zechariah, with whom Luke introduces her and with whom she is traditionally remembered; together they named the child John.

elizabeth-mother-of-john-baptist.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Elizabeth because she knew both long waiting and sudden joy. Luke tells us she and Zechariah were righteous yet had no child, and that she felt the reproach of it until God acted in her old age. When Mary arrived, Elizabeth was the first to recognize, by the Holy Spirit, who Mary's child was, and her words of blessing live on in the Hail Mary. Expectant mothers, couples hoping for a child, older people, and anyone who has waited a long time for God find her a warm companion. She also shows how to receive someone else's good news with gladness rather than envy.

quotes.text: Thus hath the Lord dealt with me in the days wherein he hath had regard to take away my reproach among men.
Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb. And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?
And blessed art thou that hast believed, because those things shall be accomplished that were spoken to thee by the Lord.

prayer.text: Lord God, you heard the prayers of Elizabeth and Zechariah and gave them John in their old age. Through St. Elizabeth's prayers, protect mothers who are expecting and the children they carry, and comfort all who long for a child. Fill me with your Holy Spirit as you filled her, so that I may recognize Christ when he comes near, often in someone I did not expect. Teach me to rejoice in other people's blessings, to speak words that encourage, and to believe that what you have promised will be fulfilled. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: Remember her with Zechariah on November 5, the traditional date; the current Roman Martyrology commemorates the two of them on September 23. Neither date is on the General Roman Calendar, so these are days for personal or family prayer.
Celebrate the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary on May 31, a feast in the General Roman Calendar whose Gospel tells of Mary's visit to Elizabeth.
Pray the Hail Mary slowly, noticing that its words "blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb" are Elizabeth's greeting.
Pray for an expectant mother you know, or offer practical help: a meal, an errand or a visit, as Mary stayed with Elizabeth about three months.
Read Luke 1:5–25 and 1:39–80, which tell her whole story in Scripture.

places.name: Basilica of the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception (St. Elizabeth Chapel)

elizabeth-mother-of-john-baptist.confirmationNote: Elizabeth is a natural Confirmation patron, because Luke says she was "filled with the Holy Ghost" when Mary greeted her, and the Spirit opened her eyes to recognize the Lord. She suits a confirmand who wants to notice God's work in others and to speak words of blessing. Her story also encourages anyone who has waited a long time for prayers to be answered.
reflectionPrompts: Whose good news could I celebrate wholeheartedly this week, the way Elizabeth rejoiced at Mary's?
Visit, call or help someone who is expecting a baby, elderly or waiting on something important.
Read Luke 1:5–80 in the Douay-Rheims and trace each time the Holy Spirit is mentioned, then compare Elizabeth's greeting with the Hail Mary.

elizabeth-of-hungary.heroSummary: St. Elizabeth of Hungary is a patron of hospitals and of the Secular Franciscan Order and Third Order Regular of St. Francis. A Hungarian princess married into the Thuringian court, she was widowed at twenty, founded a hospital at Marburg and nursed the sick herself. She died in 1231, aged twenty-four. Her memorial is November 17.
elizabeth-of-hungary.searchDescription: St. Elizabeth of Hungary (1207–1231), feast November 17: princess, young widow and Franciscan tertiary who founded a hospital at Marburg to serve the sick poor.

symbols.meaning: Her royal birth and rank as landgravine of Thuringia. Benedict XVI recalls that she once took off her crown before a crucifix, unwilling to wear gold before Christ crowned with thorns. Some images show three crowns.

symbols.symbol: Roses carried in her apron or mantle
symbols.meaning: A later legend says that bread she was secretly carrying to the poor turned into roses when she was stopped on the way. The Catholic Encyclopedia notes the same story is told of other saints; her charity itself is well documented.

symbols.symbol: Basket of bread and a flask of wine
symbols.meaning: Her daily almsgiving. During the famine of 1226 she fed large numbers of poor people from her household's stores.
The hospitals she founded, first below the Wartburg and then the Franciscan hospital at Marburg, where she spent her last years caring for patients.

elizabeth-of-hungary.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Elizabeth when they want their faith to reach the hungry, the sick and the forgotten. She was a princess who fed the poor from her own table, nursed patients with her own hands and kept going after her husband died, her position was lost and her children were placed in others' care. Catholics ask her prayers for hospital workers and caregivers, for widows and young parents who are grieving, and for families under strain. Many also turn to her when generosity draws criticism, since her charity was mocked at court. Tradition holds that even her bread became roses; the deeper wonder is her steady love.

quotes.text: Amen I say to you, as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me.
My little children, let us not love in word, nor in tongue, but in deed, and in truth.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, St. Elizabeth saw you in the poor and served you with her own hands. Through her prayers, open my eyes to the people around me who are hungry, sick or alone, and give me the courage to help them, even when it costs me comfort or approval. When grief or loss comes, keep me faithful as you kept her faithful. Bless all who care for the sick in hospitals and homes, and make our charity simple, practical and joyful. Amen.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on November 17, her obligatory memorial in the General Roman Calendar; older calendars kept her feast on November 19.
Bake bread, with children if you can, and share it with neighbors or a food pantry, as Catholic Culture suggests in memory of her care for the hungry.
Teach or review the corporal and spiritual works of mercy, and choose one to practice this week.
Learn about the Secular Franciscan Order, which honors her as a patroness, perhaps by contacting a local fraternity.
Pray for your relatives' holiness; Catholic Culture notes that her daughter and several kinswomen were drawn to holiness by her example.

places.name: St. Elizabeth's Church (Elisabethkirche) and the Elizabeth Shrine
Wartburg Castle

elizabeth-of-hungary.confirmationNote: Elizabeth suits a confirmand who wants faith to show up in practical love. She was young, newly married and surrounded by privilege, yet she spent her strength feeding the hungry and nursing the sick, even when people at court mocked her. She also lost her husband early and kept trusting God. Confirmation strengthens us to witness to Christ, and Elizabeth shows that the witness often begins with bread, time and care.
reflectionPrompts: Where do I hold back from helping someone because I worry about what others will think?
This week, volunteer an hour at a hospital, care home or food pantry, or bring a meal to someone who is sick.
Read Benedict XVI's general audience on St. Elizabeth of Hungary (October 20, 2010) alongside Matthew 25:31–46, and note how her service echoes the Gospel.

biography: the reviewed text says Ludwig died 'during the preparations for crusade'. Benedict XVI and the Catholic Encyclopedia say he had set out with Emperor Frederick II and died of fever or plague at Otranto in September 1227 before sailing, so the wording is defensible but could be sharpened. The Catholic Encyclopedia also notes that historians disagree on whether she was forced out of the Wartburg or left under moral pressure; Benedict XVI says she was driven out. The text here avoids taking sides.

elizabeth-of-portugal.heroSummary: St. Elizabeth of Portugal, called Isabel in Portugal, was a queen remembered as a peacemaker. Born a princess of Aragon in 1271, she endured an unfaithful husband, cared for the poor and sick, and more than once stopped war within her own family. Widowed, she lived as a Franciscan tertiary at Coimbra. Her optional memorial is July 4.
elizabeth-of-portugal.searchDescription: St. Elizabeth (Isabel) of Portugal (1271–1336), feast July 4: queen, peacemaker in her royal family, Franciscan tertiary at Coimbra and friend of the poor.

symbols.meaning: Her rank as queen of Portugal, which she used to give alms, found hospices and a hospital, and reach the powerful when peace was at stake.
Her work as a peacemaker, above all between King Denis and their son Afonso, and later between Portugal and Castile.
The habit she took after Denis died in 1325, when she lived beside the Poor Clare monastery she had founded at Coimbra.
A legend, told by her confraternity in Coimbra as a legend, says the bread she carried for the poor was changed into roses. A similar story is told of her great-aunt, St. Elizabeth of Hungary.

symbols.symbol: Jug, or a beggar at her side
symbols.meaning: Her steady personal service of the poor, pilgrims and the sick, in which she also involved the women of her court.

elizabeth-of-portugal.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Elizabeth of Portugal when their families are divided. She was a queen whose husband was unfaithful, whose son took up arms against his father, and whose relatives went to war with one another, and she kept working for reconciliation instead of choosing sides. Catholics ask her prayers for strained marriages, for parents and grown children who no longer speak, and for peace between nations. She also reminds us that peacemaking and care for the poor belong together. Her last journey, already old and weak, was to stop a war; she died soon after the peace was agreed.

quotes.text: Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called children of God.
If it be possible, as much as is in you, have peace with all men.

prayer.text: God of peace, you gave St. Elizabeth of Portugal patience in a hard marriage and courage to stand between those who were ready to fight. Through her prayers, heal the divisions in my family and in my heart. Where there is resentment, help me to take the first step toward reconciliation; where there is need, make me generous to the poor. Bless all who work for peace between peoples, and teach me to be gentle without being weak. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on July 4, her optional memorial in the General Roman Calendar; in the United States it moves to July 5.
Reach out to a family member you are estranged from, or pray by name for a family where there is conflict.
Read the readings the USCCB gives for her memorial, 1 John 3:14–18 and Matthew 25:31–46, and give something to a person in need.
Pray for peace in a country at war, remembering her final journey to Estremoz to stop a war between Portugal and Castile.
In Coimbra, her confraternity holds summer festas in her honor, with a penitential procession and a solemn procession in which her image is carried.

places.name: Monastery of Santa Clara-a-Nova (Church of the Queen St. Isabel), where her body rests
Monastery of Santa Clara-a-Velha, the Poor Clare house she founded

elizabeth-of-portugal.confirmationNote: Elizabeth of Portugal suits a confirmand who finds themselves in the middle of other people's conflicts. She married young into a difficult court, stayed faithful when her husband was not, and kept pressing for reconciliation in her family and between kingdoms. She also gave generously to the poor and sick. Confirmation strengthens Christians to be witnesses of Christ, and Elizabeth shows that peacemaking is one of the bravest ways to do it.
reflectionPrompts: Is there a conflict in my family or friendships where I could be a peacemaker instead of taking sides?
This week, make one concrete move toward reconciliation: a call, a note or an apology.
Read the Catholic Encyclopedia article on St. Elizabeth of Portugal and Romans 12:9–21, and note how her life puts Paul's advice into practice.

Foundress of the Poor Clares, whose monastery Elizabeth founded and lived beside at Coimbra
Shares the July 4 date on the calendar

The Coimbra confraternity gives her birth as about February 11, 1270, against 1271 in the review and the Catholic Encyclopedia; the text here uses 1271. Sources differ on whether the final peace was between her son and his son-in-law or her grandson; Alfonso XI of Castile was both, so the review's 'son and grandson' stands.

elizabeth-of-the-trinity.heroSummary: St. Elizabeth of the Trinity was a French Discalced Carmelite of Dijon whose letters and prayers teach that God lives within the soul. Born Elizabeth Catez in 1880, a gifted pianist with a fiery temper, she entered Carmel at twenty-one and died at twenty-six. Canonized in 2016, she is remembered by Carmelites on November 8.
elizabeth-of-the-trinity.searchDescription: St. Elizabeth of the Trinity (1880–1906), Carmelite feast November 8: Dijon nun and spiritual writer who taught that God dwells within the soul.
elizabeth-of-the-trinity.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Elizabeth of the Trinity when prayer feels distant or when life seems too busy for God. She discovered, first at home and then in Carmel, that God is not far away but present in the soul, waiting to be met in quiet attention. She learned this as a strong-willed girl who had to master her temper, and she held to it through a painful final illness. Catholics ask her prayers for interior peace, for perseverance in suffering, for the sick and for anyone longing to pray more simply. Her letters show that this inward life is offered to every Christian, not only to nuns.

quotes.text: I have found my heaven on earth, since heaven is God, and God is in my soul.
quotes.work: Fragment of a letter to a married friend, in The Praise of Glory: Reminiscences of Sister Elizabeth of the Trinity
quotes.translation: Benedictines of Stanbrook (London: Washbourne, 1913), public domain

quotes.text: The 'praise of glory' is a soul that contemplates God in faith and in simplicity; it reflects His whole being, and is a fathomless abyss into which He can flow and outpour Himself; a crystal through which He can shine and view His own perfections and splendour.
quotes.work: Notes written for her sister, quoted in The Praise of Glory, chapter VIII ("Laudem Gloriae")
quotes.translation: Benedictines of Stanbrook (London: Washbourne, 1913), public domain

quotes.text: That we may be unto the praise of his glory, we who before hoped in Christ.
quotes.work: Ephesians 1:12 (the verse from which she took the name "Praise of Glory")

prayer.text: O my God, Trinity Whom I adore! help me to become utterly forgetful of self, that I may establish myself in Thee, as changeless and as calm as though my soul were already in eternity. May nothing disturb my peace nor draw me forth from Thee, O my immutable Lord! but may I penetrate more deeply every moment into the depths of Thy Mystery. Give peace to my soul; make it Thy heaven, Thy cherished dwelling-place, Thy home of rest. Let me never leave Thee there alone, but keep me there all absorbed in Thee, in living faith, adoring Thee and wholly yielded up to Thy creative action.
prayer.source: St. Elizabeth of the Trinity, prayer of November 21, 1904, in The Praise of Glory, translated by the Benedictines of Stanbrook (1913), appendix, p. 260
prayer.note: The opening two paragraphs of her prayer to the Trinity, in the Stanbrook 1913 wording exactly (checked against two Internet Archive scans, 1913 and 1914). The book says the untitled prayer was found among her notes and dated November 21, 1904, the feast of the Presentation of Mary. The full prayer continues with addresses to Christ, the Word, the Holy Spirit and the Father. Modern translations begin "O my God, Trinity whom I adore, help me to forget myself entirely."

link.label: Read the full prayer in the 1913 Stanbrook translation (Internet Archive scan)

feastCustoms: Join a Carmelite community or parish for Mass on November 8, her memorial in the Carmelite calendar; it is not on the General Roman Calendar, so many parishes will not mark it.
Pray her prayer to the Trinity slowly, perhaps one phrase at a time over the day.
Spend a few minutes in silence remembering that God dwells within you, with 1 Corinthians 3:16 as a starting point.
Read a few of her letters, which she wrote to family and friends outside the cloister to share the life of prayer.
Pray for people living with chronic or painful illness, as she did through her final months.

places.name: Carmel of Flavignerot (the Carmel of Dijon, which she entered in 1901)

elizabeth-of-the-trinity.confirmationNote: Elizabeth of the Trinity suits a confirmand who wants a deeper prayer life or who struggles with a strong temper. As a girl she was known for fierce outbursts, and she learned self-mastery out of love for Christ. She came to see that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit dwell in every baptized person. Confirmation completes that baptismal gift of the Holy Spirit, and Elizabeth shows how to live attentive to God within.
reflectionPrompts: When during the day do I most forget that God is present within me, and how could I remember?
Set aside five quiet minutes each day this week to sit in silence with the Holy Trinity, without asking for anything.
Read Ephesians 1:3–14 and chapter VIII of The Praise of Glory (1913), and note why she took "Praise of Glory" as her new name.

relatedSaints.reason: A fellow French Discalced Carmelite, seven years older, whom Elizabeth recommended in her letters and prayed to in her last illness
Carmelite mystic and doctor whose writings she read and quoted often

emma.heroSummary: St. Emma of Lesum, also called Imma, was a Saxon noblewoman remembered for her generosity to the Church and to poor people. Wife of Count Liudger of the Billung family, she sought the founding of a church at Stiepel, and as a widow near Bremen she gave land and gifts. She died in 1038. Her feast is April 19.
emma.searchDescription: St. Emma of Lesum, feast April 19: Saxon noblewoman and widow (died 1038) who gave land to poor people and supported churches at Stiepel and Bremen.
emma.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Emma as a model of generosity for anyone who has money, land or influence. As a widow she could have lived only for herself; instead, the sources remember her for giving to the church at Bremen and providing land that poor people could farm, so that they could support themselves. Little is recorded of her inner life; what survives is the shape of a life spent giving. Widows, benefactors, and people deciding how to use what they own can ask her to help them give wisely and well.

quotes.text: She hath opened her hand to the needy, and stretched out her hands to the poor.
Blessed is he that understandeth concerning the needy and the poor: the Lord will deliver him in the evil day.

prayer.text: Lord God, St. Emma held land, wealth and family influence, and she used them to build up your Church and to give poor people a way to live. Through her prayers, help me see everything I have as a gift to share. Make me generous without seeking praise, and wise enough to help others stand on their own feet. Comfort widows and all who live alone after a loss, and show them how much good they can still do. Bless those who farm the land and those who work to feed others. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: Remember St. Emma on April 19, her usual commemoration; December 3, the anniversary of her death, is also kept in some calendars.
Give in a way that lasts: support a charity that helps people earn their own living, such as a community garden, farm project or job program.
Reach out to a widow or widower you know, with a visit, a meal or an invitation.
Read Proverbs 31:10–31 and think about how faith, work and generosity fit together in daily life.
In Bochum-Stiepel, Germany, the old village church, now Protestant, is linked by tradition to the church Imma had built on her estate.

places.name: Stiepel Village Church (Stiepeler Dorfkirche)

emma.confirmationNote: Emma suits a confirmand who is generous, practical and good at organizing, or who hopes to use future success to help others. She did not leave behind famous words; she left churches supported and poor families with land to work. Confirmation calls Christians to serve with the gifts they have been given, and Emma shows that wise generosity can be a lasting form of witness.
reflectionPrompts: What do I own or control, such as time, money, skills or influence, that God might be asking me to share?
This month, give something that helps a person become more independent, not only something that meets a need for one day.
Read Proverbs 31:10–31 in the Douay-Rheims and list the ways the woman described there uses her household's resources.

enda.heroSummary: St. Enda of Aran, also called Éanna or Éinne, was an early Irish monastic founder who died about 530. Tradition says he left a warrior's life, and he built a community at Killeany on Inishmore that became a school of prayer, work and Scripture for many Irish saints. His feast is March 21.
enda.searchDescription: St. Enda of Aran, feast March 21: early Irish monastic founder who built a community at Killeany on Inishmore, a school for many Irish saints. Died about 530.
enda.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Enda as one of the fathers of Irish monastic life. Tradition holds that he was once a fighting man of Oriel and that his sister Fanchea turned him toward God; whatever the details, his life shows a real change of direction. On the bare rock of Inishmore his monks prayed together, worked the land and sea, slept rough and studied Scripture so they could live it. Later Irish saints came to learn from him. Anyone seeking a simpler life, a fresh start or a deeper grounding in prayer can ask his help.

quotes.text: The Lord hath reigned, let the earth rejoice: let many islands be glad.

prayer.text: Lord God, you led St. Enda away from violence and pride to a life of prayer on the rocks of Aran, and you made his small community a school of holiness for many. Through his prayers, turn my heart toward you wherever I have taken the wrong road. Teach me to pray faithfully, to work honestly and to live simply, and to read your word so that I may live it. Bless teachers, students and all who form others in the faith, and bless the people of the islands. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: Remember St. Enda on March 21, which falls in Lent and just after St. Patrick's Day; ask whether your parish or diocese in Ireland marks it.
Take up a small piece of the Aran discipline for the day: a simple meal, a time of silence, honest manual work and a passage of Scripture read slowly.
If you visit Inishmore, go to Killeany (Cill Éinne), the village that keeps his name, where tradition places his monastery.
In Co. Louth, the parish of Killanny in the Diocese of Clogher has a church dedicated to St. Enda, a link to the tradition of his Oriel origins.
Pray for people who are trying to leave violence behind and for those who form others in prayer and learning.

places.name: St Enda's Church, Tullydrum (St Enda's Parish, Killanny, Diocese of Clogher)

enda.confirmationNote: Enda suits a confirmand who has made, or wants to make, a fresh start, or who is drawn to simplicity, the outdoors or a disciplined way of life. Tradition remembers a warrior who chose Christ instead, and history remembers the island community he built. Confirmation is a commitment to let God redirect our strength, and Enda shows that a changed life can become a place where many others learn to pray.
reflectionPrompts: Where in my life is God inviting me to change direction, as Enda did?
Choose one habit to simplify this week, such as screens, food or spending, and use the time for prayer or work for others.
Read the Catholic Encyclopedia article 'Monastic School of Aran' and note what it says about the daily rule of Enda's monks.
