prayer.text: Take, Lord, and receive all my liberty, my memory, my intellect, and all my will--all that I have and possess. Thou gavest it to me: to Thee, Lord, I return it! All is Thine, dispose of it according to all Thy will. Give me Thy love and grace, for this is enough for me.
prayer.source: St. Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises, Contemplation to Gain Love, translated by Elder Mullan, S.J. (1914)
prayer.note: Known as the Suscipe. Ignatius gives it in the Exercises as the retreatant's offering of self; many modern versions use different wording. This is Mullan's public-domain text exactly.

irenaeus-of-lyon.heroSummary: St. Irenaeus of Lyon was a second-century bishop and theologian who learned the faith from St. Polycarp in Asia Minor and later led the church of Lyon in Gaul. Against secret 'knowledge' sects, he defended the faith openly handed down from the apostles. Pope Francis named him a Doctor of the Church, the 'Doctor of Unity', in 2022.
irenaeus-of-lyon.searchDescription: St. Irenaeus of Lyon (feast June 28), disciple of Polycarp and bishop in Gaul, defended the apostles' faith and was named Doctor of Unity in 2022.
irenaeus-of-lyon.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Irenaeus when they want to understand their faith and hold on to it. He heard Polycarp, who had known the apostolic generation, and spent his life showing that the Gospel is not a secret for a clever few but the shared faith of the whole Church, taught openly everywhere. He also insisted that creation and the human body are good, made by the one God who saves us. His name comes from the Greek word for peace, and Pope Francis called him a bridge between Eastern and Western Christians. He is a natural companion in prayer for students of theology and for Christian unity.

quotes.text: For the glory of God is a living man; and the life of man consists in beholding God.
quotes.translation: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, trans. Alexander Roberts and W. H. Rambaut (1885; public domain)

quotes.text: For where the Church is, there is the Spirit of God; and where the Spirit of God is, there is the Church, and every kind of grace; but the Spirit is truth.
quotes.translation: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, trans. Alexander Roberts and W. H. Rambaut (1885; public domain)

quotes.text: the Church, having received this preaching and this faith, although scattered throughout the whole world, yet, as if occupying but one house, carefully preserves it. She also believes these points [of doctrine] just as if she had but one soul, and one and the same heart
quotes.translation: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, trans. Alexander Roberts and W. H. Rambaut (1885; public domain)

prayer.text: I do also call upon thee, Lord God of Abraham, and God of Isaac, and God of Jacob and Israel, who art the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the God who, through the abundance of Thy mercy, hast had a favour towards us, that we should know Thee, who hast made heaven and earth, who rulest over all, who art the only and the true God, above whom there is none other God; grant, by our Lord Jesus Christ, the governing power of the Holy Spirit; give to every reader of this book to know Thee, that Thou art God alone, to be strengthened in Thee, and to avoid every heretical, and godless, and impious doctrine.
prayer.source: Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book III, chapter 6, §4, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, trans. Alexander Roberts and W. H. Rambaut (1885; public domain)
prayer.note: This is Irenaeus's own prayer within Against Heresies, offered for the readers of his book; the opening word 'Wherefore' has been dropped. The Diocese of Lyon proposes the same prayer, in French, for personal and group prayer.

feastCustoms: Celebrate the memorial of St. Irenaeus at Mass on June 28; the Diocese of Lyon, which keeps the same date, honors him as its principal patron.
Pray for unity among Christians, especially between Catholics and Orthodox, in the spirit of his title 'Doctor of Unity'.
Pray the Apostles' Creed slowly; Benedict XVI connects Irenaeus's 'rule of faith' with the Creed.

He learned from Polycarp, studied the teachings of his day carefully, and answered them by pointing to the faith handed down openly in the Church. Confirmation calls Christians to bear witness to that same faith, and his name is a promise to keep learning it and to work for unity.

isaac-jogues.heroSummary: St. Isaac Jogues (1607–1646) was a French Jesuit priest who worked among the Wendat (Huron) people of New France. Captured and maimed in 1642, he escaped with Dutch help, then chose to return. He was killed in 1646 at Ossernenon, today Auriesville, New York, and is honored on October 19 among the North American Martyrs.
isaac-jogues.searchDescription: St. Isaac Jogues (1607–1646), feast October 19: French Jesuit missionary in New France, captured in 1642, killed in 1646 at Ossernenon (Auriesville, NY).
isaac-jogues.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Isaac Jogues when they need courage to go back to a hard place. After months of captivity and torture he reached safety in France, yet he asked to return to the mission. Because his hands had been mutilated, he needed papal permission even to celebrate Mass. His last known letter asks a fellow Jesuit to pray that God would enlarge his narrow heart and teach him to trust completely. He also served as an envoy of peace. Missionaries, those who suffer for their faith, and anyone called to persevere after being badly hurt find in him a companion who knew fear and went anyway.

quotes.text: I may learn to trust myself entirely to him, being very sure that he will not draw back and let me fall, when I shall cast myself lovingly into the arms of his divine and paternal providence.
quotes.work: Letter to Father André Castillon, S.J., Montreal, September 12, 1646 (Jesuit Relations, Doc. LVIII), apparently his last surviving letter
quotes.translation: English translation in Reuben Gold Thwaites, ed., The Jesuit Relations and Allied Documents, vol. 28 (Cleveland: Burrows Brothers, 1898), public domain

quotes.text: And God gave to Solomon wisdom and understanding exceeding much, and largeness of heart as the sand that is on the sea shore.
quotes.work: 3 Kings 4:29 (1 Kings 4:29), the verse Jogues echoes in Latin in that same letter when he prays for a larger heart

quotes.text: Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, you sent St. Isaac Jogues across the ocean to share your Gospel, and you gave him the courage to return to the place where he had suffered. Through his prayers, enlarge my narrow heart. When I am afraid, teach me to throw myself into the arms of your providence as he did. Bless all missionaries and all who are persecuted for your name. Make me a builder of peace between peoples, and help me to honor the dignity of every person I meet. St. Isaac Jogues and companions, pray for us. Amen.

feastCustoms: Keep October 19, when the Church honors Sts. Isaac Jogues, John de Brébeuf and companions; it is a memorial in the dioceses of the United States, while the Church in Canada celebrates the Canadian Martyrs on September 26.

Pray the Novena to the North American Martyrs published by the National Shrine of Our Lady of Martyrs in Auriesville, or make a pilgrimage there in its open season, where Jogues, René Goupil and John de la Lande were killed and St. Kateri Tekakwitha was born.
Support Catholic missions and ministries serving Native American communities, and learn about the Indigenous nations Jogues lived among rather than seeing them only through his story.
Learn the Huron Carol, the Christmas hymn attributed to his fellow martyr John de Brébeuf, as a family custom tied to these saints.

isaac-jogues.confirmationNote: Isaac Jogues suits a confirmand who has been hurt, frightened or set back and is learning to keep going. He was not fearless: his last known letter blames his own cowardice and asks for a larger heart. Yet he returned to the mission and worked as a peacemaker. Choosing him means asking the Holy Spirit for the gift of fortitude and for a trust in God that is stronger than fear.
reflectionPrompts: Where in my life am I being asked to return to something difficult, and what would it take to trust God there?
Pray this week for one missionary, or for Christians in a country where the faith is persecuted, by name if you can.

isidore-of-seville.heroSummary: St. Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636) was a bishop and Doctor of the Church who succeeded his brother Leander in Seville in 599. His Etymologies gathered classical and Christian learning into one great reference work for the Middle Ages. The Church keeps his optional memorial on April 4, the anniversary of his death.
isidore-of-seville.searchDescription: St. Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), feast April 4: bishop, Doctor of the Church and author of the Etymologies, who handed on learning to medieval Europe.

symbols.meaning: His long labor as a writer on Scripture, doctrine, history and the liturgy; Catholic Culture lists a bishop holding a pen among his images.
The Etymologies, his attempt to gather universal knowledge, which Catholic Culture says remained a favored textbook into the sixteenth century.

symbols.symbol: Shown with Leander, Fulgentius and Florentina
symbols.meaning: His family of saints: two brothers who became bishops and a sister who became an abbess, all honored by the Church.

isidore-of-seville.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Isidore when study feels slow and hard. Catholic Culture tells how, as a struggling student, he noticed grooves worn into stone by dripping water and took it as a lesson that small, steady effort leaves a lasting mark. He went on to master Latin, Greek and Hebrew and to gather the learning of his age so that others could use it. Benedict XVI also describes him torn between his love of quiet study and his duties as a bishop. Students, teachers, writers and anyone balancing prayer with a demanding job find in him a patient guide.

quotes.text: Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven, is like to a man that is a householder, who bringeth forth out of his treasure new things and old.
And it came to pass in those days, that he went out into a mountain to pray, and he passed the whole night in the prayer of God.
quotes.work: Luke 6:12 (Benedict XVI notes that Isidore pointed to Christ, who taught by day and prayed through the night, as the model for joining action and contemplation)

prayer.text: Lord God, source of all wisdom, you gave St. Isidore a love of learning and a pastor's heart. Through his prayers, help me to study with patience, to seek the truth wherever it is found, and to use what I learn in the service of others. When I am pulled between quiet prayer and the demands of work, teach me, as you taught him, to find you in both. Bless all students and teachers, and keep the Church faithful in handing on the faith from one generation to the next. St. Isidore, pray for us. Amen.

feastCustoms: Keep April 4, his optional memorial in the General Roman Calendar; when it falls in Lent it becomes a commemoration, and it is not celebrated when it falls in Holy Week or the Easter Octave.
Set a small, daily habit of study or spiritual reading and keep it faithfully, remembering the story of the water-worn stone that taught him perseverance.
Read Pope Benedict XVI's general audience of June 18, 2008, on Isidore, or listen to a talk on him from a reliable Catholic source.
If you read Latin, look into a few entries of the Etymologies to see how he organized the knowledge of his time.
Pray for students, teachers and Catholic scholars, and for unity in the faith, which Isidore and his brother Leander worked for among the Visigoths.

isidore-of-seville.confirmationNote: Isidore suits a confirmand who loves to learn, or who is learning to work hard at something that does not come easily. Choosing him means asking the Holy Spirit for the gifts of knowledge and understanding, and for the humility to put what we learn at the service of others.
reflectionPrompts: What is the 'dripping water' in my life: one small, faithful habit that could slowly shape who I become?
Choose one subject you find difficult and give it fifteen focused minutes a day this week, offering the effort to God.
Read Benedict XVI's general audience on St. Isidore of Seville (June 18, 2008) and note what he says about balancing the active and contemplative life.

isidore-the-farmer.heroSummary: St. Isidore the Farmer is the patron of farmers and of the city of Madrid. A married day laborer who worked the land of a landowner near Madrid, he is remembered for daily Mass, prayer at the plow and generosity to the poor. Canonized in 1622, he is celebrated on May 15.
isidore-the-farmer.searchDescription: St. Isidore the Farmer, feast May 15: patron of farmers and Madrid, a married farm laborer remembered for prayer, hard work and generosity to the poor.

symbols.meaning: His lifelong work as a ploughman on an estate outside Madrid, and the prayer he kept up as he worked behind the plough.
The team he ploughed with; they recall the legend, which the Catholic Encyclopedia calls a legend, that angels were seen ploughing beside him while he prayed.
The ordinary tools of a farm laborer, showing that holiness can grow in plain, daily work.

isidore-the-farmer.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Isidore because his holiness grew in the fields, not in a monastery or a palace. He was a hired laborer with a wife and a son, and tradition holds that he went to Mass early each day and prayed as he ploughed. Accounts of his life stress his care for the poor and for animals; some of the stories about him, such as angels ploughing in his place, are legends written down long after his death. Farmers, farmworkers, people in ordinary jobs and married couples ask his help, and many pray through him for good weather and a fair harvest.

quotes.text: Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth: patiently bearing till he receive the early and latter rain.
He that hath mercy on the poor, lendeth to the Lord: and he will repay him.

prayer.text: Lord God, all creation is yours, and you called St. Isidore to serve you in the fields. Through his prayers, bless the work of my hands and help me to pray in the middle of ordinary days. Bless farmers, farmworkers and all who grow our food; protect them from drought, storm and poverty, and give them a just reward for their labor. Teach me to share my table with the hungry and to care for the land and its creatures. As Isidore and Maria loved you together, strengthen every Christian family. St. Isidore, pray for us. Amen.

link.label: Novena to St. Isidore the Farmer (Catholic Culture)

feastCustoms: Keep May 15, his optional memorial in the United States; the collect for the day asks that his example move us to share our food with the hungry.

In Madrid, where he is the city's patron, the Archdiocese marks the feast with a solemn Mass at the Royal Collegiate Church of San Isidro, a procession with the images of St. Isidore and his wife St. María de la Cabeza, and a Mass and family blessings on the meadow by the saint's hermitage.

At the hermitage of San Isidro in Madrid, water from the saint's fountain is blessed and offered to pilgrims, a custom of local farmers older than the hermitage itself; legend links the spring to the saint.
Bless seeds or plant a garden, perhaps a Mary garden, since his feast falls in May, the month of Mary, using a seed-planting prayer to St. Isidore.
Pray for farmers, farmworkers and rural communities, and support a food bank or a Catholic rural-life ministry.
isidore-the-farmer.confirmationNote: Isidore suits a confirmand who works with their hands, loves the outdoors, or wonders whether an ordinary job can be holy. He never held office or wrote a book, yet the Church canonized him beside Ignatius of Loyola and Teresa of Ávila. Choosing him means asking the Holy Spirit to make daily work a place of prayer and to give a generous heart toward the poor.
reflectionPrompts: Which part of my ordinary work could I offer to God as prayer while I do it?
This week, share food with someone in need: donate to a food bank, cook for a neighbor, or invite someone to your table.
Read the Catholic Encyclopedia article 'St. Isidore the Labourer' alongside James 5:7–11, and note which details it presents as history and which as legend.

jacinta-marto.heroSummary: St. Jacinta Marto (1910–1920) was the youngest of the three shepherd children of Fátima, Portugal, who reported apparitions of Our Lady in 1917. Lively and affectionate, she offered prayers and small sacrifices for sinners and for the Holy Father. She died of influenza in a Lisbon hospital, away from her family, and was canonized with her brother Francisco in 2017.
jacinta-marto.searchDescription: St. Jacinta Marto (1910–1920), feast February 20: youngest seer of Fátima, who prayed for sinners and the pope and was canonized with Francisco in 2017.
jacinta-marto.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Jacinta when they want to love others more generously, even in small ways. The Shrine of Fátima describes a joyful child who loved flowers and lambs, shared her food with the poor, and offered her daily discomforts for the conversion of sinners. The Holy See's biography adds her love for the Holy Father. In her last illness she was taken far from home and died alone in a Lisbon hospital, accepting even that separation. Sick children, families who keep vigil in hospitals, and anyone who feels lonely in suffering find in her a tender companion.

quotes.text: Suffer the little children, and forbid them not to come to me: for the kingdom of heaven is for such.
Who now rejoice in my sufferings for you, and fill up those things that are wanting of the sufferings of Christ, in my flesh, for his body, which is the church.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, you drew the little shepherd Jacinta to love you and to care for sinners with a generous heart. Through her prayers, teach me to offer the small sacrifices of each day for others, and to pray faithfully for the Pope and the whole Church. Be near to sick children, especially those far from home, and comfort the parents who wait beside them. When I feel alone in suffering, let me remember that you are with me. Holy Mary, Our Lady of the Rosary of Fátima, pray for us. St. Jacinta, pray for us. Amen.

feastCustoms: Keep February 20, the anniversary of Jacinta's death and the liturgical feast of Sts. Francisco and Jacinta Marto; it is not on the General Roman Calendar, so check whether your parish or diocese observes it.
At the Shrine of Fátima the feast has been kept with the rosary at the Chapel of the Apparitions, a Mass in honor of the two saints, and a blessing of the children present.
Pray the rosary, as Our Lady asked of the children at Fátima, for peace in the world.
Offer one small, hidden sacrifice for others, such as giving away a treat or bearing an annoyance patiently, as Jacinta gave her own food to the poor.
Pray for the Pope, as Jacinta did, and for children who are seriously ill or in hospital far from their families.

jacinta-marto.confirmationNote: Jacinta suits a confirmand with a warm, lively heart who feels deeply for people in trouble. She was a child who loved to play, yet she learned to turn ordinary sacrifices into prayer for others and stayed faithful through a lonely illness. Choosing her means asking the Holy Spirit for compassion toward sinners and the suffering, love for the Church and the Pope, and courage when we feel alone.

jadwiga-of-poland.heroSummary: St. Jadwiga, also called Hedwig, is honored as a patron of Poland, the young queen whom St. John Paul II canonized in Kraków in 1997. Crowned in 1384, she married Grand Duke Jogaila of Lithuania, whose baptism opened his people to the Gospel, and she endowed the Kraków Academy. She died on July 17, 1399, still in her twenties.
jadwiga-of-poland.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Jadwiga when duty arrives early and asks a great deal. She was still a child when she was crowned, and she accepted a marriage she had first resisted because she believed it would serve the faith. As queen she gave generously to students, founded hospitals, and worked to keep peace with powerful neighbors. Pope John Paul II pointed to the hours she spent kneeling before the crucifix at Wawel as the source of her strength. Catholics ask her prayers for Poland and Lithuania, for students and teachers, for young leaders, and for mothers who grieve, since her infant daughter died only days before she did.

quotes.text: My little children, let us not love in word, nor in tongue, but in deed, and in truth.
It shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be the greater among you, let him be your minister: And he that will be first among you, shall be your servant.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, St. Jadwiga learned from you, kneeling before the cross, how to serve when she was young and the burdens were heavy. Through her prayers, give me courage to accept the responsibilities you place in my hands, and wisdom to use whatever I have, my time, my talents and my resources, for others. Bless students and teachers, the sick and those who care for them, and the peoples of Poland and Lithuania. Teach me to love not in word only, but in deed and in truth. Amen.

link.label: St. Jadwiga at Wawel Cathedral, where her relics are honored

feastCustoms: July 17, the anniversary of her death in 1399, is her day in the Roman Martyrology; in Poland her memorial is kept on June 8, the anniversary of her canonization in Kraków in 1997.
Pray for a while before a crucifix, as she did before the black crucifix in Wawel Cathedral; in Kraków many people visit that crucifix on pilgrimage each Good Friday.
Pray for students, teachers and Catholic universities, or help someone pay for books or tuition, remembering her bequest to the Kraków Academy, today the Jagiellonian University.
Visit or help someone who is sick, in memory of the hospitals founded under her at Biecz, Sandomierz, Sącz and Stradom.
Pray for peace between Poland, Lithuania and their neighbors, and for anyone carrying heavy responsibility at a young age.

places.name: Wawel Royal Cathedral (her tomb and the Wawel crucifix)

jadwiga-of-poland.confirmationNote: Jadwiga suits a confirmand who feels pressure to grow up quickly or who loves learning. She became ruler of Poland as a child and could have used the crown for herself. Instead she prayed, accepted hard choices for the sake of the faith, and gave her wealth to students, hospitals and the poor. Confirmation strengthens us for a mission, and Jadwiga shows that a young person's gifts can serve the whole Church.
reflectionPrompts: Where am I being asked to take on responsibility before I feel ready, and how could I bring that to God in prayer?
Give something of real value this week, such as time tutoring, a donation for a student, or a visit to someone who is sick.
Read 1 John 3:14–18 and St. John Paul II's homily for her canonization (Kraków, June 8, 1997), and note what he says she learned at the foot of the Wawel crucifix.

james-the-greater.heroSummary: St. James the Greater, son of Zebedee and brother of John, was one of the Twelve Apostles and, with Peter and John, witnessed the Transfiguration and Jesus' agony in Gethsemane. Acts 12:2 records that Herod Agrippa killed him with the sword. Tradition links him with Spain and Santiago de Compostela. His feast is July 25.
james-the-greater.searchDescription: St. James the Greater, feast July 25: son of Zebedee, brother of John, apostle killed by Herod (Acts 12:2), honored at Santiago de Compostela.

symbols.meaning: The manner of his death: Acts 12:2 records that Herod killed James, the brother of John, with the sword.
Benedict XVI explains that the staff marks him as the travelling Apostle and recalls the pilgrimage to Compostela and the pilgrimage of Christian life.

symbols.symbol: Scroll or book of the Gospel
symbols.meaning: His mission as an apostle sent to proclaim the Good News; Benedict XVI pairs it with the pilgrim's staff.
Pilgrim dress associated with the medieval and modern pilgrimage to his shrine at Santiago de Compostela; artists often show James himself dressed as a pilgrim.

james-the-greater.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. James when following Christ means leaving something secure behind. He left his father's boat and nets at a word from Jesus, and he was there both on the mountain of glory and in the garden of anguish. He and his brother once asked for places of honor, and Jesus asked whether they could drink his chalice; James became the first of the Twelve whose martyrdom Scripture records. Pilgrims on the Camino ask his company on the road, and many others ask his help to keep going when faith feels long and tiring. Tradition holds that his remains rest at Compostela.

quotes.text: And he killed James, the brother of John, with the sword.
And Jesus said to them: You know not what you ask. Can you drink of the chalice that I drink of: or be baptized with the baptism wherewith I am baptized? But they said to him: We can.
And James the son of Zebedee, and John the brother of James; and he named them Boanerges, which is, The sons of thunder.

prayer.text: St. James, you left your nets the moment Jesus called you, and you stayed with him on the mountain of glory and in the garden of sorrow. Pray for me when the road of faith is long and I am tempted to turn back. Help me to answer Christ's call without delay, to put away my wish for honor, and to drink his chalice with trust when suffering comes. Watch over all pilgrims and travelers, and bring us safely home to the Father. Amen.

link.label: The pilgrim's prayer to St. James from the Cathedral of Santiago

feastCustoms: July 25 is the Feast of St. James, Apostle, in the General Roman Calendar; he is also named in the Roman Canon of the Mass.

At Santiago de Compostela, July 25 is one of the solemnities on which the cathedral's great censer, the Botafumeiro, is traditionally swung. When July 25 falls on a Sunday, the cathedral keeps a Compostela Holy Year and opens its Holy Door.
Make a short pilgrimage to a shrine or church near you, praying along the way, as Catholic Culture suggests for his feast.
Before a journey, ask a priest for the Blessing of Pilgrims from the Book of Blessings.
Bake a Tarta de Santiago, the almond cake of Galicia, or cook a scallop dish, both traditional for his feast.

places.name: Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela (tomb of the Apostle)

james-the-greater.confirmationNote: James suits a confirmand who is energetic, ambitious or quick to act. Jesus nicknamed him and his brother 'sons of thunder', and they once asked for places of honor. Yet James learned that greatness means service, and he became the first of the Twelve to give his life for Christ. Confirmation strengthens us to witness bravely, and James shows how Christ can turn zeal into faithful courage.
reflectionPrompts: What 'nets' or securities would I find hardest to leave behind if Christ asked me to follow him more closely?
Walk to church or to a nearby shrine this week, offering the journey as a small pilgrimage for someone who needs prayer.
Read Mark 10:35–45 and Acts 12:1–3, then Benedict XVI's general audience on St. James the Greater (June 21, 2006).

relatedSaints.reason: His brother, the other son of Zebedee, called with him from their nets
With James and John, one of the three closest witnesses of the Transfiguration and Gethsemane
Fellow Galilean fisherman and apostle called on the same shore
Commemorated on the same July 25 date in the Roman Martyrology

jane-frances-de-chantal.heroSummary: St. Jane Frances de Chantal (1572–1641) was a wife, mother and widow from Dijon who, with St. Francis de Sales, founded the Visitation of Holy Mary at Annecy in 1610. The order welcomed women who were not strong enough for harsher rules, and it had grown to dozens of houses by her death. Her optional memorial is August 12.
jane-frances-de-chantal.searchDescription: St. Jane Frances de Chantal (1572–1641), feast August 12: wife, mother and widow who founded the Visitation with St. Francis de Sales in 1610.
jane-frances-de-chantal.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Jane Frances de Chantal in grief, in family strain and in seasons when prayer feels dry. Her husband was killed in a hunting accident, leaving her a young widow with children, and she spent years in a difficult household for their sake. She later lost her only son in battle and, near the end of her life, endured long interior darkness. Catholic Culture lists her as a patron of widows, of parents separated from their children and of people with in-law troubles. Many ask her help to forgive, to keep faith through loss, and to find wise spiritual direction.

quotes.text: Who shall find a valiant woman? far and from the uttermost coasts is the price of her.
And Mary rising up in those days, went into the hill country with haste into a city of Juda. And she entered into the house of Zachary, and saluted Elizabeth.
quotes.work: Luke 1:39–40 (the Visitation, which gave her order its name)

prayer.text: Lord God, you gave St. Jane Frances de Chantal a strong and faithful heart in marriage, in widowhood and in religious life. Through her prayers, comfort all who grieve, especially widows and children who have lost a parent. Help families who are divided to find patience and forgiveness. When prayer feels empty, keep me faithful as she was, trusting you in the dark. Teach me humility before you and gentleness toward my neighbor, and send me wise guides on the way to you. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: August 12 is her optional memorial in the General Roman Calendar; older calendars kept her feast on other dates, including August 21.
Read a chapter of St. Francis de Sales's Treatise on the Love of God, which he wrote with her and the Visitation sisters in mind.
Pray for widows, for children who have lost a parent and for families separated from one another, needs Catholic Culture links to her patronage.
Donate food to your parish food pantry or visit someone who is grieving, as she cared for the sick and bereaved.
If you have been putting it off, take a step toward finding a spiritual director, as she sought Francis de Sales's guidance.

jane-frances-de-chantal.confirmationNote: Jane Frances suits a confirmand who has known loss, family tension or a season when God feels far away. She buried her husband, forgave the man who caused his death, raised her children, and only then founded a religious order. Even after that, she still faced years of spiritual darkness. Confirmation strengthens us to witness in every season of life, and Jane shows that faithfulness can grow strongest in hardship.
reflectionPrompts: Is there someone I need to forgive, as Jane forgave the man whose shot killed her husband, and what first step could I take?
Reach out this week to someone who is widowed, grieving or far from family, with a call, a visit or a meal.
Read Luke 1:39–56 and the Catholic Encyclopedia article on St. Jane Frances de Chantal (1910), and note why the Visitation was founded for women who could not bear harsher rules.

januarius.heroSummary: St. Januarius, San Gennaro to the people of Naples, was a bishop of Benevento who tradition says was beheaded near Pozzuoli with his companions about 305. Naples honors him as its patron, and his feast on September 19 centers on the cathedral relic of his blood and its reported liquefaction.
januarius.searchDescription: St. Januarius (San Gennaro), feast September 19: early bishop and martyr, patron of Naples, honored for the reported liquefaction of his blood relic.

symbols.symbol: Two vials of blood resting on a book
symbols.meaning: The phials kept in Naples Cathedral that are said to hold his blood. The book is the Gospel he served as a bishop; the vials recall the devotion for which he is best known.

A detail from his late Acts: tradition holds that he was thrown into a burning furnace and the flames did not touch him. The Catholic Encyclopedia treats these Acts as untrustworthy, so this is legend rather than history.
His office as bishop of Benevento, the role in which the Church remembers him.
The usual signs of a martyr: victory won by giving his life for Christ, and the crown of glory promised to those who are faithful unto death.

januarius.whyWeTurn: Neapolitans have turned to San Gennaro for centuries when plague, war or the threat of Vesuvius hung over their city, and tradition holds that his prayers have protected them. Catholic Culture also names him a patron of blood banks and of people facing volcanic eruptions. Beyond Naples, people turn to him because he stands for courage: a bishop who, with his deacons and a lector, chose death rather than deny Christ. Little about his life can be proved, but the faith of a whole city gathered around his relic is itself a witness, and he reminds us that the Church remembers martyrs as a community.

quotes.text: Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.
And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of the testimony, and they loved not their lives unto death.

prayer.text: Lord God, you gave St. Januarius the courage to remain faithful with his companions when faithfulness cost him his life. Through his prayers, protect the people of Naples and every city that lives in the shadow of danger. Strengthen all who are afraid of disaster, and bless those who give their blood to save the lives of others. Help us to love you more than our own safety, and to stand by our brothers and sisters when witnessing to you is hard. We ask this through Christ our Lord. Amen.
prayer.note: The collect for his memorial in the Roman Missal is a copyrighted ICEL text, so an original prayer is given here.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on September 19, his optional memorial in the General Roman Calendar, and pray for the people of Naples.

In Naples, the archbishop exposes the reliquary of his blood in the cathedral on his feast, and also on the Saturday before the first Sunday in May and on December 16; many people follow the celebration online or on television.
If you live near New York, join the Feast of San Gennaro in lower Manhattan, which Catholic Culture recommends to readers who live nearby.
Share a Neapolitan meal with family or friends, a custom Catholic Culture suggests for his day.
Give blood, or help at a blood drive, remembering the martyr whose relic is his blood.

januarius.confirmationNote: Januarius suits a confirmand who wants courage to stand firm for the faith, or who has roots in Naples and southern Italy. He was a bishop who did not die alone but with his deacons and lay companions, a reminder that faith is lived in community. Choosing him means asking for steadiness under pressure and loyalty to the people God has placed beside you.
reflectionPrompts: When has fear kept me quiet about my faith, and whom could I ask to stand with me next time?
Find out whether you are eligible to give blood, and schedule a donation or help at a parish blood drive.
Read the 1910 Catholic Encyclopedia article on St. Januarius and note what it says can and cannot be known about his life and about the relic.

jeanne-jugan.heroSummary: St. Jeanne Jugan (1792–1879) was a Breton servant and nurse who, in the winter of 1839, carried a blind, infirm elderly woman home and gave her her own bed. That act began the Little Sisters of the Poor. Later set aside and forgotten as foundress, she was canonized in 2009. Her feast is August 30.
jeanne-jugan.searchDescription: St. Jeanne Jugan (1792–1879), feast August 30: Breton foundress of the Little Sisters of the Poor, who began by giving an elderly woman her own bed.
jeanne-jugan.whyWeTurn: People turn to Jeanne Jugan when they are caring for an aging parent, worried about growing old alone, or working in homes for the elderly. She knew poverty from childhood and never had much education, yet she saw Christ in old people whom others overlooked. She also knew what it is to be pushed aside: for decades the younger sisters did not know she had founded their community. Benedict XVI, canonizing her, pointed to her humility and joyful trust in Providence. She reminds us that small acts of hospitality matter, and that hidden faithfulness is never wasted.

quotes.text: Amen I say to you, as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me.
Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
quotes.work: Matthew 5:3, from the Beatitudes in which Benedict XVI saw the root of her trust in Providence

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, you were welcomed in the poor old woman whom St. Jeanne Jugan carried home and laid in her own bed. Through her prayers, open my door and my heart to the elderly who are lonely, sick or forgotten. Give patience and joy to all who care for them, and to me when I grow old, give trust in your Providence. When I am overlooked, keep me humble and faithful, as she remained hidden for so many years. Bless the Little Sisters of the Poor and the people they serve. Amen.
prayer.note: The Little Sisters of the Poor publish a novena prayer, a litany and other devotions to St. Jeanne Jugan on their website.

Pray the novena prayer or the litany of St. Jeanne Jugan published by the Little Sisters in the days leading up to her feast.
Visit, call or write to an older relative or neighbor who lives alone, in the spirit of her first act of hospitality.
Volunteer at, or give to, a home that cares for elderly people with limited means.
Read Benedict XVI's homily from her canonization on October 11, 2009, when Damien of Molokai was canonized with her.

jeanne-jugan.confirmationNote: Jeanne Jugan suits a confirmand who loves grandparents or older neighbors, is drawn to nursing or caregiving, or feels unnoticed. She had little schooling and no influence, but she opened her home to someone in need and trusted God with the rest. Choosing her means committing to see Christ in the elderly and to serve faithfully even when no one gives you credit.
reflectionPrompts: Who is the older person in my life who might feel forgotten, and what would it look like to make room for them?
This week, spend an hour with an elderly relative or neighbor, or help at a home for the elderly.

jerome.heroSummary: St. Jerome (about 347–419/420) was a priest, scholar and Doctor of the Church who learned Greek and Hebrew so that the Latin Church could read the Scriptures more faithfully. His translations became much of the Vulgate. He spent his last decades in Bethlehem, and his feast is September 30.
jerome.searchDescription: St. Jerome, feast September 30: priest, Doctor of the Church and biblical translator whose work shaped the Vulgate, the Latin Bible of the West.

symbols.meaning: A later legend tells that he drew a thorn from a lion's paw at his monastery and the lion stayed with him. It is a story, not history, but it pictures the strength and the gentleness his work required.

An anachronism, since cardinals as we know them came later; artists used it to recall his service to Pope Damasus in Rome. It is often shown laid aside, which Catholic Culture reads as his rejection of ecclesiastical pomp.

symbols.symbol: Book or Bible, with a pen
symbols.meaning: His lifelong work of translating and explaining the Scriptures.
Penance: he is shown as an aged hermit beating his breast with a stone, recalling his ascetic years in the desert and his struggle against his own temper and pride.
Reminders that life is short, kept before the eyes of a scholar who wanted his study to lead to conversion.

jerome.whyWeTurn: People turn to Jerome when they want to understand the Bible and not just own one. Students, teachers, translators and librarians ask his help with hard, patient work. He is also a saint for anyone with a sharp tongue: his letters show a brilliant, quarrelsome man who still spent his life serving God's word. He taught that not knowing the Scriptures means not knowing Christ, a line the Second Vatican Council quoted in Dei Verbum. And he insisted that study should change how we treat the poor. Jerome reminds us that holiness can grow in a difficult temperament.

quotes.text: Read the divine scriptures constantly; never, indeed, let the sacred volume be out of your hand. Learn what you have to teach.
quotes.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 6 (1893), public domain

quotes.text: Read often, learn all that you can. Let sleep overcome you, the roll still in your hands; when your head falls, let it be on the sacred page.
quotes.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 6 (1893), public domain

quotes.text: love the knowledge of scripture, and you will no longer love the sins of the flesh.
quotes.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 6 (1893), public domain

prayer.text: Lord God, you gave St. Jerome a great love for your word and the patience to spend his life making it known. Through his prayers, give me a hunger for the Scriptures, so that by knowing them I may come to know Christ. Teach me to read slowly and to let what I read change how I live, especially how I treat the poor. Where I am quick to anger or proud of what I know, make me humble and gentle. Bless all who teach, translate and study your word. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
prayer.note: The line about knowing the Scriptures echoes Jerome's Commentary on Isaiah, Prologue, as cited in Dei Verbum 25 and in Pope Francis's apostolic letter for the 1600th anniversary of his death.

link.label: Pope Francis, Scripturae Sacrae Affectus (September 30, 2020)

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on September 30, his memorial in the General Roman Calendar.
Begin or renew a habit of reading Scripture every day, even one chapter, as Catholic Culture suggests for his feast.
Read part of Pope Francis's apostolic letter Scripturae Sacrae Affectus, signed on his feast in 2020 for the 1600th anniversary of his death.
Read one of his letters, such as Letter 52 to Nepotian or Letter 107 to Laeta on teaching a child, in the public-domain Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.
Make a quiet examination of conscience about anger and harsh words, a struggle Jerome's own letters reveal.

places.name: Church of St. Catherine, Bethlehem, beside the Basilica of the Nativity, with the grottoes linked to the memory of St. Jerome

jerome.confirmationNote: Jerome suits a confirmand who loves languages, reading or hard questions, or who struggles with a quick temper. He spent decades learning Hebrew and Greek so others could hear God's word, and his letters show he was far from perfect. Choosing him means committing to know Christ through the Scriptures and to let that knowledge make you more patient and more generous.
reflectionPrompts: When did I last read Scripture for its own sake rather than only hearing it at Mass, and what keeps me from it?
Choose one Gospel and read a chapter each day until you finish it.
Read Jerome's Letter 52 to Nepotian (NPNF, Second Series, vol. 6) and note what he says about preaching, practice and the poor.

joachim.heroSummary: St. Joachim is honored by tradition as the father of the Virgin Mary, husband of St. Anne and grandfather of Jesus. Scripture never names him: his name and the story of his long wait for a child come from the second-century Protoevangelium of James. The Church celebrates Joachim and Anne together on July 26.

symbols.symbol: Lamb, or a lamb brought to the altar
symbols.meaning: The offering he brought to the Temple. In the Protoevangelium he is told he may not offer first because he has no child; later legend turns this into a priest refusing his gift.
Another image of his Temple offerings and of the prayer for a child that, in the tradition, God answered.
The Protoevangelium pictures him as a wealthy man with flocks who withdrew to the wilderness to fast and pray for forty days.
Later tradition places his joyful meeting with Anne here after angels announce Mary's birth; the Protoevangelium says only that Anne stood 'by the gate'.
His place as Mary's father, who in the tradition presents her to the priests for a blessing and later brings her to the Temple.

joachim.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Joachim as a father and grandfather, someone who waited, prayed and handed on faith. Scripture tells us nothing about him, not even his name; the story comes from an early noncanonical writing and long devotion. In that story he is shamed for having no child, goes into the wilderness to fast, and refuses to eat until God answers him. Tradition holds that the answer was Mary. Fathers, grandfathers, couples longing for children and anyone carrying a long, unanswered prayer find in him a steady companion. With Anne, he reminds the Church that grandparents are often where faith first takes root.

quotes.text: But these were men of mercy, whose godly deeds have not failed: Good things continue with their seed, Their posterity are a holy inheritance, and their seed hath stood in the covenants.
quotes.work: Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 44:10–12, chosen for context; it is not about Joachim

quotes.text: And mayest thou see thy children's children, peace upon Israel.
quotes.work: Psalm 127:6 (Psalm 128:6 in modern numbering), chosen for context; it is not about Joachim

prayer.text: Lord God, the Church has long honored St. Joachim as the father of the Virgin Mary and the grandfather of your Son. Through his prayers, bless fathers and grandfathers, and all who wait a long time for an answer from you. Give them patience when you seem silent, humility when they feel overlooked, and joy in the gifts you send. Help us to honor the older people in our lives and to receive the faith they hand on, so that our families may be places where your promises are remembered. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on July 26, the memorial of Sts. Joachim and Anne, parents of the Blessed Virgin Mary; when it falls on a Sunday, the Sunday liturgy takes its place.
Honor your grandparents on the day, a long custom tied to this feast: visit, call or pray with them, or remember them at Mass if they have died.

Keep the World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly, which Pope Francis set on the fourth Sunday of July near this feast; some bishops' conferences, including in the United States, observe it on another Sunday.
Pray especially for fathers, grandfathers and couples longing for a child.
In the Byzantine tradition, Eastern Catholics honor Joachim and Anne on September 9, the day after the Nativity of Mary.
joachim.confirmationNote: Joachim suits a confirmand who is grateful for a father, grandfather or godparent who handed on the faith. Nothing he said or did is recorded in Scripture, so choosing him is a choice to honor patient, hidden faithfulness and prayer that keeps going when answers are slow. Confirmation strengthens Christians to witness to Christ, and much of that witness happens in families, from one generation to the next.
reflectionPrompts: What prayer have I been carrying for a long time, and can I offer it to God again today with trust?
Thank a father, grandfather or older mentor this week for something he taught you about faith.
Read the Catholic Encyclopedia article on St. Joachim and chapters 1–5 of the Protoevangelium of James, noting what the Encyclopedia treats as uncertain.

relatedSaints.reason: His wife in tradition; they share the July 26 feast
Husband of his daughter Mary and fellow member of Jesus' family
Mary's kinswoman, whose long-childless family also received a child as God's gift
A canonized father remembered for handing on faith to his daughters

joan-of-arc.heroSummary: St. Joan of Arc is honored by many Catholics as a patron of prisoners and captives, fitting for a young woman who spent her final year in custody. Raised at Domremy, she believed God called her to aid Charles VII. She was condemned and burned in 1431, cleared in 1456, and canonized in 1920.
joan-of-arc.searchDescription: St. Joan of Arc (1412–1431), feast May 30: the young Frenchwoman who answered God's call, was tried and burned at Rouen, and was canonized in 1920.

symbols.symbol: White banner with lilies and the names "Jhesus Maria"
symbols.meaning: At her trial Joan described her own standard: white cloth sprinkled with lilies, the world shown with an angel on each side, and the names of Jesus and Mary. She said she carried it into battle and valued it far above her sword.
Her documented place in the 1429 campaign that relieved Orléans and led to Charles VII's coronation at Reims; artists usually show her as a young woman in armor.
Her military role, though she testified that she had never killed anyone and carried her banner in attacks for that reason.
The French crown she served; she testified that the king granted her brothers arms bearing two golden lilies and a sword.
Her execution by burning at Rouen in May 1431, after a trial later annulled in 1456.

joan-of-arc.whyWeTurn: People turn to Joan when they feel small against forces far larger than themselves. She was a teenager with no rank or schooling, yet she trusted that God could use her. Her trial record lets us hear her own voice: frightened at times, but honest, quick, and unwilling to claim more about her soul than she knew. Because she spent her last year as a prisoner and was condemned by a court later found unjust, many Catholics ask her prayers for prisoners, captives, and anyone wrongly accused. Others look to her for courage to keep faith with their conscience under pressure.

quotes.text: If I am not, may God place me there; if I am, may God so keep me. I should be the saddest in all the world if I knew that I were not in the grace of God.
quotes.work: Trial of Condemnation, public examination of February 24, 1431 (answering whether she knew she was in God's grace)
quotes.translation: T. Douglas Murray, ed., Jeanne d'Arc, Maid of Orleans (1902), public domain

quotes.text: Better, forty times better, my banner than my sword!
quotes.work: Trial of Condemnation, public examination of February 27, 1431
quotes.translation: T. Douglas Murray, ed., Jeanne d'Arc, Maid of Orleans (1902), public domain

quotes.text: It was I, myself, who bore this banner, when I attacked the enemy, to save killing any one, for I have never killed any one.
quotes.work: Trial of Condemnation, public examination of February 27, 1431
quotes.translation: T. Douglas Murray, ed., Jeanne d'Arc, Maid of Orleans (1902), public domain

prayer.text: Saint Joan of Arc, you trusted God when you were young, unknown, and afraid, and you kept calling on the name of Jesus to the very end. Pray for all who are imprisoned, held captive, or wrongly accused, that they may find mercy, justice, and hope. Pray for me when I must speak the truth before people who misunderstand me. Help me to stay honest without bitterness, brave without pride, and humble enough to say only what I truly know. Ask the Lord to keep me in his grace, and if I have strayed from it, to bring me back. Amen.

feastCustoms: May 30, the anniversary of her death, is her commemoration in the Roman Martyrology rather than a memorial on the General Roman Calendar; ask her intercession at a weekday Mass or in personal prayer.
Pray slowly with the Holy Name of Jesus, the name Joan called on as she died, for example by praying the Litany of the Holy Name.
Pray for prisoners, captives, and people awaiting trial, and consider supporting a parish or diocesan prison ministry.
In Orléans, the cathedral celebrates a solemn Mass in her honor each May 8 during the city's festivities marking its liberation in 1429.
Read a few of her answers from the trial record and notice how she spoke about God, conscience, and grace.

places.name: Cathedral of Sainte-Croix, Orléans

joan-of-arc.confirmationNote: Joan can be a strong Confirmation saint for someone who feels young or overlooked but wants to act on faith. She asks the confirmed to listen for God's call, to pray steadily, and to tell the truth even when it costs something. Choosing her also means learning her real history, including her trial and the Church's later reversal of its verdict, rather than only the heroic legend.
reflectionPrompts: Joan refused to claim certainty she did not have about her own soul. Where am I tempted to overstate or hide the truth about myself before God?
Write a short note, offer a prayer, or give practical support this week to someone who is in prison or feels trapped by circumstances.
Read her answers from the February 24, 1431 examination in T. Douglas Murray's 1902 translation of the trial record and note how she responds to trick questions.

john-baptist-de-la-salle.heroSummary: St. John Baptist de La Salle was a French priest of Reims who gave up a comfortable canonry to live with schoolteachers and train them. The community he formed became the Brothers of the Christian Schools. Named patron of Christian educators and teachers in 1950, he is remembered on April 7.
john-baptist-de-la-salle.searchDescription: St. John Baptist de La Salle (1651–1719), feast April 7: founder of the Brothers of the Christian Schools and patron of teachers and Christian educators.
john-baptist-de-la-salle.whyWeTurn: Teachers turn to St. John Baptist de La Salle because he understood their work from the inside. He did not set out to found anything; he began by helping a few struggling schoolmasters and slowly found himself sharing their table, their poverty and their mission. He opened schools for poor children, trained teachers, ran Sunday courses for young workers and kept going through lawsuits and opposition from people who should have supported him. Catholics ask his prayers for patience in the classroom, for wisdom with difficult pupils and for the courage to keep serving children whom others overlook. Parents and catechists also find in him a friend who took teaching seriously as a way to holiness.

quotes.text: But they that are learned shall shine as the brightness of the firmament: and they that instruct many to justice, as stars for all eternity.
Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not; for of such is the kingdom of God.

prayer.text: Lord God, you called St. John Baptist de La Salle away from comfort and status to serve poor children and the teachers who taught them. Through his prayers, bless every teacher, catechist and parent who forms young people. Give them patience on hard days, wisdom with children who struggle, and joy in work that is often unseen. Help me to remember that I stand in your holy presence wherever I learn or teach, and to treat each young person as someone you love. Live, Jesus, in our hearts for ever. Amen.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on April 7, his memorial in the General Roman Calendar; when April 7 falls in Holy Week or the Easter Octave, the memorial is not celebrated that year.
Lasallian schools and the Brothers of the Christian Schools also celebrate him on May 15, the anniversary of his 1950 proclamation as patron of Christian educators.
Thank a teacher who shaped you, by letter or in person, and pray for the teachers in your parish school or your family's schools.
End a prayer with the Lasallian invocation "Live, Jesus, in our hearts", answered with "Forever!", as Lasallian communities and schools do.
Read a Church document on Catholic education, such as the Congregation for Catholic Education's Consecrated Persons and Their Mission in Schools, which Catholic Culture suggests for his day.

john-baptist-de-la-salle.confirmationNote: John Baptist de La Salle suits a confirmand who hopes to teach, coach, tutor or help younger people learn. He let God redirect a secure life, one step at a time, until he was living with teachers and serving poor children. Confirmation calls Christians to share their faith in words and in service, and De La Salle shows that patient, ordinary work with young people can be a real way of witnessing to Christ.
reflectionPrompts: Who taught me something that changed my life, and have I ever thanked them or prayed for them?
This week, offer to help a younger person with schoolwork, a skill or a question about faith.
Read Daniel 12:1–3 and Mark 10:13–16 in the Douay-Rheims, then read the founder's biography on the Brothers' site, lasalle.org, and note what made him change course.

john-baptist-de-rossi.heroSummary: St. John Baptist de Rossi was an eighteenth-century Roman priest who spent his life among the people the city overlooked: drovers and farm laborers, the sick in hospital, prisoners and homeless women. Though he lived with epilepsy, he became one of Rome's most sought-after confessors. His memory is kept on May 23.
john-baptist-de-rossi.searchDescription: St. John Baptist de Rossi (1698–1764), feast May 23: Roman priest and confessor who served laborers, the sick, prisoners and homeless women despite epilepsy.
john-baptist-de-rossi.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. John Baptist de Rossi because he never let illness or awkward schedules keep him from the people who needed him. Epilepsy limited him, and for years he held back from hearing confessions, yet once encouraged he spent long days in the confessional and became known as a second Philip Neri. He went to the drovers and herdsmen at the old Roman Forum at hours they could manage, visited the sick at the hospital of St. Galla, and opened a refuge for those who wandered the streets at night. Catholics ask his help when they feel too weak to serve, and when they hope to make God's mercy easier for others to reach.

quotes.text: Come to me, all you that labour, and are burdened, and I will refresh you.
The Spirit of the Lord is upon me. Wherefore he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor, he hath sent me to heal the contrite of heart,

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, you gave St. John Baptist de Rossi a heart for workers, the sick, prisoners and the homeless of Rome, and you made his weakness a place where your mercy could work. Through his prayers, help me to go where people are rather than waiting for them to come to me. Give strength to all who live with chronic illness or epilepsy, and patience to those who care for them. Bless priests who hear confessions, and make me humble and honest when I come to you for forgiveness. Amen.

feastCustoms: Remember him on May 23, the day he died in 1764; he is not on the General Roman Calendar, but his relics rest in the Roman parish church dedicated to him, where his altar is a focus of local devotion.
Go to confession, or pray for the priests who hear confessions in your parish, recalling that he became a tireless confessor once he overcame his hesitation.
Visit or call someone who is sick, in hospital or living with a chronic illness.
Support a shelter or refuge for homeless women or people with nowhere to sleep, as he helped found one in Rome.
Pray for workers whose hours keep them from parish life, and think of one way your community could reach them.
john-baptist-de-rossi.confirmationNote: John Baptist de Rossi suits a confirmand who lives with an illness or limitation, or who feels drawn to people others pass by. Epilepsy shaped his whole life, yet he went out to laborers, the sick, prisoners and homeless people, and helped many return to God through confession. Confirmation strengthens Christians to witness where they are, and he shows that weakness need not stop anyone from serving.
reflectionPrompts: Who in my own city or neighborhood is easy for me to overlook, and what would it take for me to notice them the way this priest noticed people others passed by?
This week, make room in my schedule for one person who needs patience more than advice, and listen without hurrying them.
Read Luke 4:16–21 slowly, then note one phrase from Jesus’ words in the synagogue that describes the kind of ministry de Rossi chose.

john-berchmans.heroSummary: St. John Berchmans was a Flemish Jesuit student who died in Rome in 1621, aged twenty-two, before he could be ordained. Fellow Jesuits remembered the care he gave to prayer, study, and the ordinary duties of community life. Jesuits celebrate him on November 26, and many altar servers and students look to him as a model.
john-berchmans.searchDescription: St. John Berchmans, Jesuit student who died at 22 in 1621, remembered for doing ordinary duties with great care. Symbols, prayer and November 26 feast.

symbols.meaning: His love for Christ crucified; as he was dying he asked for his crucifix, and his statues show him holding it.
His faithful keeping of the rule of the Society of Jesus, which the Catholic Encyclopedia singles out as the mark of his holiness.
His devotion to Mary; the rosary was among the three things he asked to hold at the end, and it appears in his statues.

john-berchmans.whyWeTurn: People turn to John Berchmans because his holiness was ordinary in the best sense. He never preached a famous sermon or traveled as a missionary. He studied hard, kept the rule of his community, prayed the rosary, and stayed kind to those around him, even after losing both parents during his years of formation. The Catholic Encyclopedia describes him as a saint who did ordinary actions with extraordinary perfection. That makes him a natural companion for students, altar servers, and anyone tempted to think small duties do not matter. Asking his prayers is a way of asking for faithfulness in whatever is in front of you today.

quotes.text: If I do not become a saint when I am young, I shall never become one.
quotes.work: Saying recorded in the Catholic Encyclopedia, "St. John Berchmans" (1910)

quotes.text: My penance is to live the common life.
quotes.work: Saying recorded in the Catholic Encyclopedia, "St. John Berchmans" (1910)

quotes.text: He that is faithful in that which is least, is faithful also in that which is greater.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, you made Saint John Berchmans holy in the middle of classes, chores, and community life. Through his prayers, help me do the small things in front of me with care and love: my studies, my work, my promises, and my prayers. When no one notices, remind me that you do. Keep me close to you on the cross and close to your Mother in the rosary, and make me faithful to the commitments I have made. Give young people the courage to want holiness now, not someday. Amen.

feastCustoms: Jesuit communities and schools keep his feast on November 26; the Roman Martyrology also remembers him on August 13, the day he died in 1621.
Pray for and thank the altar servers in your parish; Catholic Culture lists him as a patron of altar servers and young people.

john-bosco.heroSummary: St. John Bosco is a patron of young people and schoolchildren, the Turin priest Pope John Paul II called father and teacher of youth. Don Bosco gathered poor and working boys into an oratory of prayer, learning and play, and founded the Salesians and, with Maria Mazzarello, the Salesian Sisters. His memorial is January 31.
john-bosco.searchDescription: St. John Bosco (1815–1888), feast January 31: Turin priest, founder of the Salesians and 'father and teacher of youth', known for his Preventive System.
john-bosco.whyWeTurn: People turn to Don Bosco because he believed no young person was a lost cause. Salesian accounts tell of a dream he described from age nine, which he took as a call to dedicate himself to educating the young. In Turin he gathered apprentices, street boys and young workers into an oratory where they could pray, learn a trade, study and play. His Preventive System asked educators to rely on reason, religion and loving kindness, and to be present with the young rather than ruling by punishment. Parents, teachers, youth ministers and young people themselves ask his prayers for a child who is struggling, for patience, and for joy in sharing the faith.

quotes.text: And the king of Sodom said to Abram: Give me the persons, and the rest take to thyself.
quotes.work: Genesis 14:21 (in Latin 'Da mihi animas, cetera tolle', which Don Bosco took as his motto, 'Give me souls, take all the rest')

quotes.text: Charity is patient, is kind: ... Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.
quotes.work: 1 Corinthians 13:4, 7 (the words of St. Paul on which Don Bosco said his Preventive System is based)

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, you gave St. John Bosco a father's heart for poor and restless young people, and you taught him to win them with reason, faith and kindness. Through his prayers, protect the children and teenagers I love, especially any who are lost, lonely or in trouble. Give parents, teachers and youth leaders patience, good humor and a steady presence. Teach me to seek souls more than comfort, as he did. Mary, Help of Christians, whom he trusted in everything, pray for us. Amen.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on January 31, his memorial in the General Roman Calendar; Salesian schools and parishes often keep it as a festive day.
Do something fun with children that also teaches, such as a magic trick, juggling, a puppet show or a story with a lesson, as Catholic Culture suggests in memory of how he drew children to catechism.
Pray to Mary, Help of Christians, the title of Mary he spread and for whom he built the Turin basilica where his remains now rest.
Read a few pages of his 1877 treatise on the Preventive System and choose one way to be more patient and present with a young person.
Pray for, or support, a youth center, Salesian school or mission that serves poor young people.

john-bosco.confirmationNote: John Bosco suits a confirmand who loves being with people, enjoys games and music, or wants to help younger kids find their way. Confirmation strengthens Christians to witness with courage and joy, and Don Bosco shows that the Gospel can be shared on a playground as well as in church.

john-cantius.heroSummary: St. John of Kanty, or John Cantius, is a patron of Poland and Lithuania. A priest and professor at the University of Kraków in the fifteenth century, he copied books by hand, taught philosophy and theology, and was known for giving his own food and clothes to poor students. His feast is December 23.
john-cantius.searchDescription: St. John of Kanty (John Cantius, 1390–1473), feast December 23: Kraków priest and professor known for scholarship and generosity to poor students.
john-cantius.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. John of Kanty because he held together two things we often keep apart: serious study and practical love. He spent decades teaching at the Kraków Academy and patiently copying manuscripts, yet he also noticed when a student was hungry or cold, and he gave away what he had. His Kraków parish remembers him as a patron of teachers, scholars and young people, and of works of mercy. Students, teachers and researchers ask his prayers for diligence and honesty in their work, and anyone tempted to treat knowledge as a way to feel superior finds in him a gentle correction: learning is meant to serve others.

quotes.text: Knowledge puffeth up; but charity edifieth.
Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful.

prayer.text: Lord God, you gave St. John of Kanty a mind eager for truth and a heart quick to share with the poor. Through his prayers, help me to study and work with patience and honesty, and keep me from using what I know to make myself look greater than others. Open my eyes to students, coworkers and neighbors who are struggling, and make me generous in helping them. Bless teachers, scholars and the people of Poland and Lithuania. Amen.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on December 23, his optional memorial in the General Roman Calendar; in Poland and in some older calendars he is celebrated on October 20.
Do a work of mercy before Christmas: prepare a food or gift basket for a family in need, or give through your parish or a St. Vincent de Paul group, as Catholic Culture suggests for his day.
Help a student who is struggling, with tutoring, books, a meal or simply encouragement.
Visit someone who is lonely during the holidays, such as a neighbor or a resident of a nursing home.
Learn about Polish Catholic culture, or cook a Polish dish such as pierogi with your family.

Confirmation gives Christians gifts such as knowledge, understanding and counsel for the good of others, and John shows how those gifts are meant to be used.

john-chrysostom.heroSummary: St. John Chrysostom (about 349–407) was a priest of Antioch and later bishop of Constantinople, whose preaching earned him the name "golden-mouthed." A Doctor of the Church, he pressed for reform, organized care for the poor and died in exile. The Roman Church remembers him on September 13; Byzantine calendars commonly use November 13.
john-chrysostom.searchDescription: St. John Chrysostom (about 349–407), feast September 13: the "golden-mouthed" preacher, bishop of Constantinople and Doctor of the Church who died in exile.
john-chrysostom.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. John Chrysostom when faith has to reach both the pulpit and the street. He preached through whole books of Scripture, explaining them so that ordinary listeners could live by them. He insisted that honoring Christ in church means little if we ignore Christ in the hungry and the stranger, and as bishop he simplified his household and organized help for people in need. That honesty cost him his see and finally his life in exile. Preachers, teachers, public speakers and anyone trying to tell the truth with love find in him a bold and practical companion in prayer.

quotes.text: Wouldest thou do honor to Christ's body? Neglect Him not when naked; do not while here thou honorest Him with silken garments, neglect Him perishing without of cold and nakedness.
quotes.work: Homilies on the Gospel of Matthew, Homily 50, section 4 (on Matthew 14:23–36)
quotes.translation: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, vol. 10, Homilies on Matthew, trans. George Prevost, rev. M. B. Riddle (1888; public domain)

quotes.text: Since God hath no need at all of golden vessels, but of golden souls.
quotes.work: Homilies on the Gospel of Matthew, Homily 50, section 4
quotes.translation: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, vol. 10, Homilies on Matthew, trans. George Prevost, rev. M. B. Riddle (1888; public domain)

quotes.text: Amen I say to you, as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me.
quotes.work: Matthew 25:40, the saying of Christ that Chrysostom draws on in that same passage

prayer.text: Lord Jesus Christ, you gave St. John Chrysostom a golden tongue to open the Scriptures and a brave heart to speak the truth. Through his prayers, teach me to honor you not only at your altar but in every hungry, cold or forgotten person I meet. Give preachers and teachers clear words and humble hearts. When telling the truth costs me something, keep me steady and free from bitterness. And in good days and hard ones, let me say with him: glory be to God for all things. Amen.

feastCustoms: Keep the memorial of St. John Chrysostom, Bishop and Doctor of the Church, on September 13 in the Roman calendar; Byzantine Churches, Catholic and Orthodox, commonly keep his feast on November 13.
Attend the Divine Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom at an Eastern Catholic parish; the principal Eucharistic liturgy of the Byzantine tradition bears his name.
Read Homily 50 on Matthew and do one concrete work of mercy for someone hungry, cold or alone, as he urged.
Practice speaking well: Catholic Culture suggests imitating this patron of orators by learning to give a speech, perhaps in a family speech contest.

john-chrysostom.confirmationNote: John Chrysostom suits a confirmand who loves words, whether in debate, writing or speaking, and wants to use them for God. He trained in rhetoric, then put that gift at the service of the Gospel and the poor. He also shows that courage can be quiet and costly: he kept preaching the truth when it brought exile. Choosing him means asking the Holy Spirit for the gifts of counsel and fortitude.
reflectionPrompts: Where do I honor Christ with words or gestures while overlooking him in someone near me who is in need?
This week, give one hour or one meal to someone who is hungry or alone, and do it quietly.

john-climacus.heroSummary: St. John Climacus was a monk and later abbot of Mount Sinai, probably in the late sixth and seventh centuries. He is named for his book The Ladder of Divine Ascent, thirty steps from renouncing sin to perfect love. Catholics recall him on March 30, and Byzantine Churches also honor him on the Fourth Sunday of Lent.
john-climacus.searchDescription: St. John Climacus, feast March 30: abbot of Mount Sinai and author of The Ladder of Divine Ascent, a 30-step guide from renunciation to love.
john-climacus.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. John Climacus when they want to grow in the spiritual life one honest step at a time. He spent decades in prayer as a hermit near Sinai, yet others kept seeking his advice, and he became abbot before returning to solitude. His Ladder looks plainly at anger, gluttony, pride and discouragement, and treats each as a wound to be healed rather than a reason to despair. It ends not in a feat of discipline but in faith, hope and above all love. Monks, penitents, anyone fighting a stubborn habit and anyone keeping Lent find in him a patient, experienced guide.

quotes.text: And he saw in his sleep a ladder standing upon the earth, and the top thereof touching heaven: the angels also of God ascending and descending by it.
quotes.work: Genesis 28:12, Jacob's ladder, the biblical image of ascent to God

quotes.text: And now there remain faith, hope, and charity, these three: but the greatest of these is charity.
quotes.work: 1 Corinthians 13:13, the triad to which the Ladder's thirtieth and final step is devoted, as Benedict XVI notes

prayer.text: Lord Jesus Christ, you called St. John Climacus to climb toward you step by step in the silence of Sinai. Through his prayers, help me to see my faults honestly without losing heart, and to take the next small step you ask of me today. Heal what is wounded in me, humble what is proud, and teach me to remember you with every breath. Lead me past fear and discouragement to faith, hope and charity, and above all to love for you and for my neighbor. Amen.

feastCustoms: Remember him on March 30, his day in the Church's list of saints (Vatican News marks him as a saint of that day); he has no memorial on the General Roman Calendar, so in the Roman Church this is mostly a personal or monastic observance.
Byzantine Churches, including Eastern Catholic Churches, also honor him on the Fourth Sunday of Lent; attend that Sunday's Divine Liturgy at an Eastern Catholic parish if you can.
Read the Ladder slowly during Lent, as monastic readers have long done, perhaps one of its thirty steps a day.
Practice the short prayer of the heart Benedict XVI describes from the Ladder: repeat the name of Jesus quietly, in rhythm with your breathing.
Read Benedict XVI's general audience of 11 February 2009 on him, a short introduction to the Ladder.

john-climacus.confirmationNote: John Climacus suits a confirmand who wants a practical plan for growing closer to God. His Ladder treats holiness as a climb taken one step at a time, with honest attention to habits that hold us back. Yet he insists that the top of the ladder is love, not mere self-discipline. Choosing him means asking the Holy Spirit for perseverance, humility and a heart that keeps rising toward charity.
reflectionPrompts: Which one habit is holding me back most right now, and what small first step could I take against it?
Set a brief daily time this week to pray the name of Jesus quietly, in rhythm with your breathing.
Read Benedict XVI's general audience of 11 February 2009 on St. John Climacus, then read the final step of the Ladder on faith, hope and charity.

The Fourth Sunday of Lent observance comes from the reviewed feast note; 'monastic readers have long read it in Lent' follows the reviewed biography's 'continuing place in Lenten and monastic reading'.
